Every New Apple Product Launching in 2027 and beyond
In the sections below we’ve split the upcoming new products into categories including Mac, iPad, iPhone, Apple Watch, Home, AirPods, and some new product categories.


						

							







What new iPhones are coming in 2027?
Reports point to a split iPhone launch schedule in 2027, with the iPhone 18, iPhone 18e and potentially an updated iPhone Air arriving in spring. A major redesign could follow in the fall to mark the iPhone’s 20th anniversary. There is a lot of speculation about whether Apple will use the iPhone 19 or iPhone 20 name.

				
					

				
			There are new iPhones coming.
Foundry




iPhone 18 & iPhone 18e
Spring 2027 launch expected
The iPhone 18 and 18e are rumored to arrive together in the spring of 2027. Both could gain A20 chips and more RAM. The iPhone 18 is expected to retain dual rear cameras and gain a 24MP selfie camera; the 18e may keep one rear camera and a 60Hz display. Read about the iPhone 18 and iPhone 18e rumors. 
iPhone Air 2
First half of 2027 rumored
The iPhone Air could also be getting an update. But there are rumors that it will actually merge with the iPhone 18. See our iPhone Air 2 rumors.
iPhone 19 or 20 – 20th anniversary iPhone 
Apple’s 20th-anniversary iPhone could feature curved glass, ultra-thin bezels and two larger display sizes. Under-display Face ID could reduce the camera cutout. See our iPhone 19 or 20 rumors – because one thing nobody is sure about is whether Apple will skip 19 like it skipped 9 with the arrival of the iPhone X. 
Should you buy now or wait? 
If you need an iPhone now, compare current models with discounted older stock and refurbished alternatives. If your existing phone still meets your needs and you’re considering a standard or lower-cost model, waiting for the rumored spring 2027 launches may give you more choice. See our guide to When is the best time to buy an iPhone.


						

							


Which new iPads are coming in 2027?
Apple is reportedly planning updates to the entry-level iPad, iPad Air and iPad Pro in the first half of 2027. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the Air could gain an OLED display, while the Pro is expected to offer faster performance and vapor-chamber cooling. 

				
					

				
			
Screenshot

Foundry




iPad (12th generation)
First half of 2027 rumored
When Apple updated the standard iPad in March 2025, the biggest disappointment was its A16 chip, which doesn’t support Apple Intelligence. The next model is expected to address that with an A18 or A19 chip, bringing Apple’s AI features to its entry-level tablet.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman previously predicted a 2026 launch but now expects the new iPad in the first quarter of 2027 at the earliest. Read more in our new iPad rumor roundup.
iPad Air
First half of 2027 rumored
The next iPad Air could gain an OLED display, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. That would make screen quality a potentially significant part of this update, alongside any processor improvements.
iPad Pro
First half of 2027 rumored
Gurman also expects a faster iPad Pro with vapor-chamber cooling. The cooling system could help manage heat during gaming and demanding AI tasks. 
Should you buy now or wait? 
With the iPad prices increasing in June 2026, you may want to hold off buying one now. If you are going to pay more at least get the most up-to-date model, or buy from Apple’s Refurbished Store to get a bargain. Read Should I buy an iPad now or wait?


						

							


Which new Macs are coming in 2027?
2026 was a significant year for the Mac, with Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro and a new entry-level laptop – the MacBook Neo. What is in store for 2027?
MacBook Air with M6 
Now that the MacBook Pro, iMac and Mac mini have the M6 chip, it’s only a matter of time before the MacBook Air gets its processor upgrade. 
MacBook Neo 
Currently, the MacBook Neo is powered by the A18 Pro chip. We expect it will get an upgrade to the A20 Pro chip that powers the iPad mini. 
A larger iMac

				
					

				
			The iMac Pro with its large display and powerful processor is missed. 
Apple




Apple has launched the M6 iMac, but could there be something bigger coming? Reports suggest Apple has explored a new iMac Pro with a 32-inch mini-LED display. Pro-level performance is rumored, with more powerful chips and greater memory capacity than the standard model.
Read about the larger iMac rumors.
Should you buy now or wait? 
With the prices of Macs increasing in June due to the global RAM shortages you may want to hold off buying one now. If you are going to pay more at least get the most up-to-date model, or buy from Apple’s Refurbished Store to get a bargain. Read the following for more guidance:
Should you buy the MacBook Pro now or wait? 
Should you buy the MacBook Air now or wait?
Should you buy a Mac mini now or wait?
Should you buy a Mac Studio now or wait?


						

							


New AirPods coming in 2027

				
					

				
			
Apple




AirPods with a camera?
According to a brief update in Mark Gurman’s Power On newsletter for Bloomberg in August, Apple is aiming to launch camera-equipped AirPods.
The new earbuds are expected to resemble the AirPods Pro 3, although it’s not yet clear whether they will also include a heart rate sensor.
The cameras are said to include both visible-light and infrared sensors, but they reportedly won’t be designed for taking photos or recording video, as their placement and image quality would make them unsuitable for those tasks. Instead, the cameras are expected to enable AI-powered features, such as hand gesture recognition, adapting audio based on the surrounding environment, and detecting whether someone is speaking directly to you or simply talking nearby.
Wondering whether to buy AirPods? Read Should I buy AirPods now and our AirPods buying guide. 


						

							


Software updates
Apple released iOS 27, iPadOS 27, macOS 27 and its other major updates in September 2026, introducing Siri AI, expanded Apple Intelligence features, new parental controls and app improvements. Further point updates will bring additional features, refinements and bug fixes.
For current features, availability and forthcoming additions, see our macOS 27 and iOS 27 guides. Our separate  latest iOS beta and latest macOS beta guides track testing of future updates.
Siri and Apple Intelligence
Siri AI brings more natural conversations, personal-context and onscreen awareness, and more actions across apps. Not every promised Siri AI feature was available at launch. 
October’s 27.2 updates added French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish alongside English. Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish and Vietnamese are due by year-end. In the EU, Siri AI is available on macOS but remains unavailable on iOS, iPadOS and watchOS.
Availability depends on device, language and region, and some users may need to join a waiting list.
iOS 28, iPadOS 28, macOS 28
Apple is expected to preview its next major operating systems at WWDC in June 2027, followed by summer beta testing and public releases in the fall.


						

							


Apple smart-home products coming in 2027 and beyond
In October 2026 Apple announced a major expansion of its smart-home lineup with the launch of the HomeView, HomePod mini 2, a new Apple TV 4K and the Apple Home Collection at its “Welcome Home” experience. We are still waiting for the update to the larger HomePod, with hope that could arrive in 2027.

				
					

				
			
Screenshot

Foundry




HomePod 3
Expected: 2027 
The HomePod mini was updated in 2026, but not the larger HomePod. The reason for the delay may be that a more advanced HomePod speaker featuring a built-in display is coming. 
HomeView Ultra
Possible release: Late 2027 at the earliest, potentially 2028, according to The Information.
Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple is developing a higher-end HomeView, codenamed J595, with a 9-inch display mounted on a motorized arm. The screen could rotate through 360 degrees and automatically turn toward whoever is speaking.
A November 2 report from The Information suggests the device could cost around $1,000 and arrive in late 2027 at the earliest, although its launch could slip into 2028. Development of its autonomous AI features reportedly remains a constraint, with Apple still deciding which capabilities to include in the first-generation model. Cameras and sensors could allow it to respond to its surroundings – for example, turning on lights when someone enters a room.
This would be a separate, more advanced model than the 7-inch HomeView announced in October 2026. Apple has not announced the device, and “HomeView Max” and “HomeView Ultra” remain speculative names. Read more about the HomeView Ultra here: ‘HomeView Ultra’ with robot arm may be coming next year


						

							


Upcoming Vision devices, AR and spatial computing
Apple Smart Glasses 
Possible 2026 introduction, 2027 launch
Unlike the bulky Vision Pro headset, the upcoming smart glasses from Apple are expected to follow a form factor similar to the Ray-Ban Meta glasses. Said to be built specifically for “Visual Intelligence.” It will likely handle tasks such as live translations, music playback, phone calls, and turn-by-turn directions. Apple could provide a first glimpse or “preview” of the glasses by the end of 2026.
Vision Pro
Possible 2027 update
Prior to 2026, Apple’s spatial computing strategy has focused on the high-end market, but reports indicate a more affordable version of the headset is in development. Apple has reportedly paused work on a successor to the high-end Vision Pro and could instead release a cheaper Vision Pro.


						

							


Apple products announced in 2026
Here is what Apple has announced in 2026:
MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display: Bringing OLED touchscreens, Dynamic Island and a thinner, lighter design to 14-inch and 16-inch M5 Pro/Max models. 
MacBook Pro M6: A standard, non-touchscreen MacBook Pro; M6 performance upgrade, Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.
iMac M6: M6 and connectivity upgrades; existing 24-inch design and seven colors retained.
iPad mini: 8.5-inch OLED display, thinner and lighter design, water and dust resistance, landscape Center Stage camera.
HomeView: A new smart-home display with a 7-inch touchscreen, available in tabletop and wall-mounted versions.
HomePod mini 2: An updated speaker with an S10 chip, new colors and Siri AI coming through a future software update.
Apple TV 4K: A fourth-generation model with an A19 chip and an updated Siri Remote.
Apple Home Collection: Cameras, doorbells, locks and thermostats developed with accessory partners.
iPhone Duo: Apple’s first foldable iPhone: iPhone Duo Guide.
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max: A20 Pro chip, upgraded vapor-chamber cooling, camera improvements: iPhone 18 Pro & Max Guide.
Apple Watch Series 12 & Ultra 4: Faster chips, Apple’s latest health-sensing features: Apple Watch Series 12 & Ultra 4.
AirPods 5: Stronger open-ear Active Noise Cancellation and longer battery life: AirPods 5.
Mac mini M6 and M5 Pro: Faster storage, upgraded connectivity, and a strong focus on AI performance: New Mac mini 2026 guide.
Mac Studio M5 Max and M5 Ultra: Faster AI and graphics performance, increased memory bandwidth: New Mac Studio 2026 guide.
AirPods Max 2: Improved audio and the H2 chip. Find out more here: AirPods Max 2 guide.
MacBook Neo: Apple’s brand new, low-cost Mac laptop. Find out more here: MacBook Neo guide.
MacBook Air M5: Now with the M5 chip. Read about the 2026 MacBook Air here: MacBook Air M5 guide.
MacBook Pro M5 Pro & M5 Max: A significant upgrade over the M4 series. Read: MacBook Pro M5 Pro & Max guide.
Studio Display: Finally gets Thunderbolt 5 and a better webcam. 
Studio Display XDR: With mini-LED technology and ProMotion up to 120Hz.
iPhone 17e: The new, entry-level, iPhone replaces the iPhone 16e. Read more here: iPhone 17e guide.
iPad Air M4: The iPad Air now has an M4 chip. Read more here: iPad Air M4 guide.
AirTag 2: Four years on Apple updated the AirTag, read our review here: AirTag 2nd gen review.
And… RIP Mac Pro: Apple has confirmed that it is discontinuing its tower workstation.  


						

							





What Apple launched in 2025
Here’s a quick look at what Apple released in 2025:
February 2025: iPhone 16E – the replacement for the iPhone SE and iPhone 14 brought Apple Intelligence support to the entry-level iPhone.
March 2025: iPad Air M3 and A16 iPad launched on March 4 and MacBook Air M4 and M4 Max Mac Studio on March 5.
September 2025: Apple introduced four new iPhones: iPhone 17, 17 Pro, 17 Pro Max, and the iPhone Air. We also saw the new AirPods Pro 3 and three new Apple Watches: the Series 11, Ultra 3 and SE 3.
October 2025: Apple announced a new M5 processor and released the M5 MacBook Pro, M5 iPad Pro, and an update to the Vision Pro, featuring the new chip.
What Apple launched in 2024

The M3 MacBook Air launched on March 4.
The M2 iPad Air, the M4 iPad Pro, and the Apple Pencil Pro all launched on May 7.

Apple hit the ground running in 2023 and closed the year with the Vision Pro, although it didn’t arrive until 2024:

title: Apple's Q4 2026 Earnings Call Takeaways
content:
Apple held its earnings call for the fourth fiscal quarter of 2026 today, and it was Apple CEO John Ternus' first earnings call in his new role. He had Apple CFO Kevan Parekh on hand, and he brought in Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan.


The trio covered iPhone Duo sales, Siri AI, and increasing memory costs, among other topics.

iPhone Duo

After the earnings release, Ternus told Reuters that Apple isn't able to meet demand for the ‌iPhone Duo‌, and there's no word on when supply/demand balance will be reached.

Ternus also acknowledged display issues and said a "very small percentage" of units have been returned.

iCloud+

Ternus reiterated Apple's plans to add usage limits on server-side AI features like ‌Siri‌ AI and photo editing. Users who need more capacity will be able to purchase expanded access, but there's still no pricing information or details on the limits included with each iCloud+ plan.

When asked about token consumption, Parekh said it's still early days on how much is done on-device vs. with Private Cloud Compute.
The mix of [on-device and cloud Siri] is very early days, and so it's hard to predict exactly what the mix of those costs are going to look like. Obviously, on device, you know, it's very very efficient. No real costs associated with that. But on the server side, we have some inference costs.



Siri AI

Ternus said Apple has real room to expand ‌Siri‌'s capabilities over time, and that Apple wants customers to be aware of what AI agents have access to.
As far as agentic capabilities, you know, we think these are promising tools for users. We just want to make sure that users are aware of what they're giving access to. We want to make sure this is done in a way that protects security and privacy. So, you know, we're pushing really hard on that with Siri AI, but we're also really encouraged by the fact that Apple devices are the best places to use all forms of AI.

He also said Apple's privacy focus differentiates it from other AI providers.
I mean, if you think about it, so much of your personal data is on your iPhone. You know, whether it's your contacts, your communications, health data, financial data, all of that, and Siri can tap into that and help you access it in a way that's very secure and private, and that nobody else has access to. Even Apple doesn't have access to it, and so we think that is a core kind of differentiator that we're excited about, and we're going to continue to push on that.


iOS and macOS Merging

With the MacBook Pro gaining a touch display, an analyst asked if we're going to see a single unified operating system in the future.

Ternus said Apple tries to make the best version of each and every product, while also adding features like Handoff that span across devices, but the company has no plans to make major changes.
If you look at what we did last week with the MacBook Pro, we took a huge leap forward. These MacBook Pros are better in every way than the ones that came before them, and we're really proud of that. And so we don't have any fundamentally different changes that we're planning right now. Nor would we talk about it anyway.


China

Revenue in Greater China was up 21 percent during the quarter, which was a quarterly record. Performance was primarily driven by the iPhone and the Mac.

Install Base

Apple has more than 2.5 billion active devices.

Memory

Ternus said the memory situation is "unprecedented," and Apple expects even higher memory costs in the December quarter. Apple's price increases in June and September offset some of the pressure, as do lower costs from some non-memory components and carry-in inventory.

memory prices will continue to increase.

Supply Constraints

iPhone, iPad, and Mac were constrained in the September quarter, which Khan said was driven by demand combined with limited availability of the advanced nodes SoCs are produced on. He said constraints on advanced nodes are easing with the transition of more of the lineup to 2nm chips.

iPhone

iPhone revenue was $57.6 billion, up 17 percent year over year and a new September quarter record.

iPhone 18 alongside the iPhone 18 Pro, Pro Max, and ‌iPhone Duo‌, but he skirted the question.

Mac

Revenue was $10.8 billion, up from $8.7 billion, despite supply constraints. Full-year Mac revenue was $37.9 billion, up from $33.7 billion in 2025. Ternus said Apple has never sold more Macs in a fiscal year than it did in 2026.

iPad

‌iPad‌ revenue was down in the quarter, coming in at $6.2 billion, down from $7 billion in the year-ago quarter. Apple said revenue was down because of supply constraints and a difficult compare against the launch of the A16 ‌iPad‌ last year.

Services

Services revenue hit $31.6 billion, up from $28.8 billion in the year-ago quarter, and a new all-time record. In 2026, services revenue was $123.3 billion.

App Store saw a record number of nearly a billion average weekly visitors, and Apple saw growth in the number of users who are paying for at least one service.

Wearables

Wearables, Home, and Accessories revenue was $8.3 billion, down 8 percent year over year. There was a difficult compare against the launch of the Apple Watch SE 3 and AirPods Pro 3 in 2025.

Apple TV 4K, the HomePod mini, and the Apple HomeView didn't ship during the September quarter.

December Quarter

Apple expects revenue to grow 7 to 10 percent year over year, leading to the best quarter for revenue in Apple's history. Services revenue is expected to grow between 8 and 9 percent.

Gross margin is expected to be between 45 and 46 percent, impacted by higher memory costs and costs related to the ramp of ‌Siri‌ AI.

title: Apple Dodges Question on More Price Hikes as Memory Costs Climb
content:
Apple expects memory costs to continue to increase in the December quarter and beyond, CEO John Ternus said during today's earnings call. Ternus, COO Sabih Khan, and CFO Kevan Parekh all commented on Apple's struggle with memory.


"What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented," said Ternus. He said Apple saw higher memory costs in the September quarter, and the December quarter will be worse. "Looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase," he said.

Apple was able to offset September costs by using memory it stockpiled at lower prices and securing lower prices on some non-memory components. Apple expects the same factors to cover some of the December increases, along with price increases on iPads, Macs, and iPhones in June and September.

An analyst asked if prices could increase again, but Khan, who took the question, avoided offering a direct answer. Parekh said Apple's price increases were done "reluctantly" and the company is trying to balance the impact.
I think what we try to do is evaluate, and in doing that, we evaluate the unit's revenue margin, and we're really being thoughtful and deliberate at evaluating kind of the short-term and long-term considerations. And we really believe we're balancing this well.

Ternus said Apple expects a declining benefit from pre-purchasing memory over time. Apple's inventory more than doubled year over year to $14.5 billion, which suggests Apple is buying up memory before prices go up yet again. "As we work to improve supply, our manufacturing purchase obligations have increased by $33 billion from June to the September quarter, which you'll see in our annual filing when it comes out tomorrow," he said.

Siri AI costs. Mac and iPad supplies will be constrained in the December quarter because of memory issues.

title: Apple posts record revenue on strong iPhone, Mac sales
content:
Macworld





After a jam-packed month that included the launch of a new smart-home display, touch-screen laptop, and folding phone, Apple on Monday released impressive quarterly results leading into what should be a stellar holiday quarter. For the quarter ending September 30, which notably doesn’t include any of the above products, Apple posted revenue of  $114.5 billion, a 12 percent increase over the same quarter last year and a massive close to its “best fiscal year ever,” according to CEO John Ternus. 
Leading the way, as expected, was iPhone sales. With the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro boosting the numbers, Apple posted 57.5 billion in revenue compared to 49 billion last year, a 17 percent increase. The quarter includes roughly two weeks of iPhone 18 Pro preorders and sales, but doesn’t include any iPhone Duo orders, which didn’t go on sale until October 16.
Also hitting shelves this quarter was the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, but those didn’t have nearly as big of an impact. Sales in the Wearable, Home, and Accessories category were down about 8 percent year-over-year despite the new products. Also down was iPad revenue, which posted an 11 percent decline. The new OLED iPad mini could help stabilize things in the fourth quarter, but the rest of the iPad lineup isn’t expected to get an update until 2027.
The opposite is true for the Mac. Buoyed by the launch of the M6 Mac mini and M5 Ultra Mac Studio, Apple posted a strong 25 percent increase year-over-year with earnings of $10.8 billion. Ternus said that Apple has, “never sold more Macs in a fiscal year.” 
That bodes well for the holiday quarter, when the new M6 iMac and MacBook Pro, as well as the new PROLED XDR MacBook arrive. Apple expects revenue to grow 7-10 percent despite “constrained supply,” which would be the best quarter for revenue in the company’s history.
Finally, Apple’s Services category continues to grow. For the first time, Apple topped $30 billion in revenue for Services on growth of around 10 percent.
Apple is holding a conference call at 5 pm ET to discuss the results and the road ahead for its fiscal 2027, so stay tuned for updates.

title: Apple CEO Ternus Says iPhone Duo Shortages Have No End Date in Sight
content:
Apple is unable to meet demand for the iPhone Duo and there's no timeline for when the company will catch up, CEO John Ternus told Reuters following today's earnings report.


Duo is constrained as of today. The ramp is going well, and we're working hard to get it to as many customers as quickly as possible, but at this point, we're not able to predict when supply and demand will be in balance.

title: Apple Reports 4Q 2026 Results: $30.7B Profit on $114.5B Revenue
content:
Apple today announced financial results for the fourth fiscal quarter of 2026, which corresponds to the third calendar quarter of the year. The quarter included a number of August and September product releases from Apple, as well as the CEO transition from Tim Cook to John Ternus that took place on September 1.


For the quarter, Apple posted revenue of $114.5 billion and net quarterly profit of $30.7 billion, or $2.10 per diluted share, compared to revenue of $102.5 billion and net quarterly profit of $27.5 billion, or $1.85 per diluted share, in the year-ago quarter.

Gross margin for the most recent quarter was 47.9 percent, compared to 47.2 percent in the year-ago quarter. Apple also declared a quarterly dividend payment of $0.27 per share, payable on November 16 to shareholders of record as of November 12.

Apple set September quarter records for total revenue, iPhone revenue, and earnings per share, and an all-time record for Services revenue.

"Today, Apple is proud to report a September quarter revenue record of $114.5 billion, up 12 percent from a year ago, with iPhone reaching a September quarter record and Services reaching an all-time high, capping off our best fiscal year ever," said John Ternus, Apple's CEO. "We're closing the year with our most ambitious lineup yet. That includes the iPhone Duo, the most transformational iPhone since the original, alongside iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, our most powerful iPhones yet. We also just introduced a whole new generation of hardware for the home and brought Touch to Mac for the first time. Together with the all-new Siri AI, it's an incredible lineup to carry us into the holiday season."



Apple will provide live streaming of its fiscal Q4 2026 financial results conference call at 2:00 pm Pacific, and MacRumors will update this story with coverage of the conference call highlights.

Conference call recap ahead...



1:39 pm: Apple's share price is down about a quarter of a percentage point in after-hours trading following the earnings release, after dropping 1.8% in regular trading today.

1:40 pm: "Apple delivered September quarter records for net income and EPS. Our record September quarter capped off a strong fiscal 2026, with all-time record revenue of $479 billion and double-digit EPS growth," said Kevan Parekh, Apple's CFO. "We generated $28 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter, allowing us to return $28 billion to shareholders. Thanks to our very high levels of customer satisfaction and loyalty, our installed base of active devices reached a new all-time high across all major product categories and geographic segments."

1:42 pm: Year-over-year revenue change by product segment: Mac up 23.7%, iPhone up 17.5%, Services up 9.8%, Wearables down 7.9%, and iPad down 10.4%.

1:44 pm: Revenue performance by geographic segment: Greater China up 21.0%, Rest of Asia Pacific up 15.0%, Europe up 11.5%, Americas up 10.2%, and Japan down 1.4%.

1:58 pm: Apple's quarterly earnings call with analysts will begin momentarily. Expected on the call are Apple CEO John Ternus and CFO Kevan Parekh.

2:00 pm: The call is beginning.

2:02 pm: We're starting with the standard notices about forward-looking statements from investor relations head Suhasini Chandramouli. "Apple assumes no obligation to update any forward-looking statements, which speak only as of the date they are made."

2:02 pm: John: "Hello, everyone, and thanks for joining us. It's a privilege to be with you for the first time as Apple CEO. I'm honored to represent our teams and the work they do every day."

2:03 pm: "Today, Apple is pleased to report $114.5 billion in revenue, up 12% from a year ago, and a September quarter record. These results helped Apple achieve its best ever fiscal year for revenue and EPS."

2:04 pm: He's going over recent launches, including the iPhone 18 Pro and Duo, as well as the touch MacBook Pro, new iMac and ‌iPad‌ Mini, and new Apple Watch and AirPods models, and the new smart home products.

2:05 pm: "I'm feeling great about the opportunities ahead for Apple, from our product roadmap and broad range of services to promising areas like health, emerging markets, enterprise, and education. As one example, we recently secured our biggest education deal ever for Mac with the Department of Education in the Philippines. They're going to deploy 170,000 MacBook Neos to teachers and staff."

2:06 pm: "Apple is the greatest company in the world, we've assembled an extraordinary collection of talent: the best engineers, designers, developers, and experts in every corner of our business, from our supply chain to our stores. Every day, we bring the right people together with the best ideas to build products and services that change lives. Guided by a foundational set of values and a belief that the best technology should make a better world. We do that by making products that are powerful and intuitive and meet Apple's uncompromising standards for quality, performance, design, and durability. That's the Apple experience customers love."

2:06 pm: "Apple Services amplify the experience of every device, helping people work, play, listen, watch, and stay connected to the world around them. I'm delighted with where our services business is today and where it's going. And with an installed base of more than 2.5 billion active devices, I'm looking forward to expanding our offerings and improving the lives of users around the world."

2:07 pm: "We see tremendous opportunity in AI as well. Siri AI marks a new chapter in AI at Apple. It is a completely reimagined assistant that is powerful, personal, private, and deeply relevant to our users' daily lives. ‌Siri‌ AI picks up what's relevant to our users, understands what's on their screen, and holds a natural conversation, all to help them with the things they do every day. It's the ‌Siri‌ we've always wanted."

2:07 pm: "We are very pleased with the reviews and feedback we've received, and we're so excited that more and more users are getting to experience it."

2:07 pm: "Then there's Mac, which is having an AI moment all its own. Mac is what brought me to Apple, and through the years, it has opened a world of possibilities. More than 40 years after the first Mac, the category is having its biggest moment yet."

2:08 pm: "From Mac to iPhone to ‌iPad‌, we are proud that our products are the best platforms in the industry for AI, for both first-party and third-party applications, and we're excited about the opportunities that creates. Ultimately, everything we do at Apple is for our users."

2:08 pm: "We had an excellent quarter at Apple. In addition to September quarter and fiscal year records in total company revenue, iPhone set a September quarter revenue record, capping its best fiscal year ever."

2:09 pm: "Services achieved an all-time record during the quarter to close out our best year ever there too. We grew in the vast majority of markets we track, setting September quarter records in the Americas, Europe, Greater China, and the rest of Asia Pacific. We also set September quarter revenue records in both developed and emerging markets. In addition to an all-time record in India."

2:09 pm: "iPhone revenue was $57.6 billion for the September quarter, up 17% from a year ago, despite supply constraints and foreign exchange headwinds, we grew strong double digits in the U.S. and Greater China to achieve September quarter revenue records. We also set a September quarter record for upgraders worldwide, as well as in the U.S., China Mainland, and India, helping to deliver our best fiscal year ever for upgraders globally."

2:10 pm: He's back to touting the strong response to the ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ and Duo.

2:12 pm: "Turning to Mac, revenue was $10.8 billion, up 24% from a year ago, despite supply constraints. We had double-digit growth in the majority of markets we track, and particularly strong performance in our emerging markets, where we set a September quarter revenue record. We also set a September quarter record for customers new to the Mac. According to IDC, we gained share globally during the quarter and for the full fiscal year, and we have never sold more Macs in a fiscal year than we did this time, which is a truly remarkable testament to these incredible products."

2:12 pm: He's again going over the recent Mac announcements.

2:13 pm: "Now turning to ‌iPad‌, where revenue was $6.2 billion for the September quarter." Then he began talking about the new iPad mini, without elaborating on ‌iPad‌'s numbers.

2:13 pm: "In Wearables, Home, and Accessories, revenue was $8.3 billion for the September quarter." He then went into talking about the new products that were recently launched.

2:15 pm: "Services revenue was $31.6 billion, up 10% from a year ago, and an all-time record. We saw double-digit growth in the majority of markets that we track, and we set all-time revenue records in the Americas and Europe, as well as the September quarter record in the rest of Asia Pacific."

2:16 pm: "Turning to Apple Pay, we recently launched in India with Access Bank, bringing a seamless, safe, and secure way to pay in one of the biggest markets in the world. Today, ‌Apple Pay‌ is available in over 90 markets, giving customers around the world peace of mind built into every transaction."

2:17 pm: "People love Apple products and services for the countless ways they make life easier, more enjoyable, and just plain better. They also count on Apple to create technology responsibly, built the right way, not the easy way."

2:18 pm: "We're also pleased to be doing more and more manufacturing in the United States through our American Manufacturing Program. We're deepening partnerships with suppliers across the country... Nearly 100 components in our newest iPhones come from American companies in more than a dozen states. All told, Apple supports more than 450,000 American jobs with 1000s of suppliers and partners across all 50 states."

2:18 pm: "I am proud of what we've accomplished this quarter, and I'm excited for what's ahead. ahead. We have everything we need to be extraordinarily successful, and with this team, this vision, this mission, and these values, I have no doubt that we will."

2:18 pm: We're switching to Kevan now for more details into the numbers.

2:19 pm: "Our revenue of $114.5 billion was up 12% year over year, a September quarter revenue record. This strong performance was despite sequential foreign exchange headwinds of nearly two percentage points, as well as supply constraints on iPhone, Mac, and ‌iPad‌."

2:19 pm: "Products revenue was $82.9 billion, up 12 percent year over year, driven by strong double-digit growth on iPhone and Mac. Our install base of over two and a half billion active devices has reached another all-time high across all major product categories and geographic segments."

2:20 pm: "Services revenue was $31.6 billion, up 10 percent year over year. We saw strong performance in many services categories, with all-time records in video, cloud services, payment services, and advertising, and a September quarter record in music."

2:20 pm: "Company gross margin was 47.9%, and products gross margin was 37.2%. These both included a benefit from tariff refunds, which had a favorable impact of approximately one percentage point in the September quarter. When you remove the tariff refunds from both the June and September quarter, both company and products gross margin would be down about one point sequentially, primarily driven by higher memory costs. As of the September quarter, we have received the vast majority of the refunds related to tariffs paid. Services gross margin was 76%, up 40 basis points sequentially."

2:21 pm: "Operating expenses came in at $19.2 billion, up 21% year over year as we continued to make investments in R and D. Net income was $37 billion. Diluted earnings per share was $2.10, up 14% year over year, and included five cents of favorable impact from tariff refunds. Both net income and EPS set September quarter records, even when excluding the tariff refund benefit. Operating cash flow was also very strong at $28.1 billion."

2:21 pm: "This performance marked our best fiscal year yet, with $478.8 billion in revenue, up 15% year over year, and a fiscal year record for EPS of $8.98, up 20% year over year."

2:22 pm: "iPhone revenue was $57.6 billion, up 17 percent year over year, despite supply constraints. We grew double digits in the majority of markets we track, and we also reached September quarter revenue records across both developed and emerging markets. As John mentioned, it was a record year for the total company, and we also had our best year ever for iPhone, both worldwide and in every geographic segment. The iPhone active install base grew to an all-time high, and iPhone had a record year for upgraders globally and in several markets, including the U.S., China mainland, India, and Japan. According to a recent survey from World Panel, iPhone was a top-selling model in the U.S., urban China, India, the UK, Germany, Australia, and Japan."

2:23 pm: "Mac revenue was $10.8 billion, up 24% year over year, despite supply constraints. This performance was driven by the strength of the MacBook Neo and ‌MacBook Pro‌. We saw double-digit growth in both developed and emerging markets, with all-time records in markets like India and Southeast Asia. Emerging markets continued to see strong performance on Mac, resulting in Mac's best fiscal year there, driven by record upgraders and customers new to the Mac."

2:23 pm: "‌iPad‌ revenue was $6.2 billion, down 10% year over year, driven by the supply constraints I mentioned earlier, as well as a continued difficult compare against the launch of the A16-powered ‌iPad‌ in the prior year. The ‌iPad‌ install base reached an all-time high during the quarter, and over half of the customers who purchase an ‌iPad‌ were new to the product."

2:23 pm: "Wearables, Home and Accessories revenue was $8.3 billion, down 8% year-over-year as we face a difficult compare against the launch of the Watch SE 3 and the AirPods Pro 3 in the prior year. The wearables install base reached a new all-time high in over half of customers who bought an Apple Watch in the quarter were new to the product."

2:24 pm: "Services revenue set an all-time record of $31.6 billion, up 10%. year over year, despite over one and a half points of sequential FX headwinds. We set all-time revenue records in the majority of markets we track, including several emerging markets like Latin America and India. We are optimistic about the long-term future of our services business, with our large install base of over two and a half billion active devices, we have an incredibly strong foundation for growth opportunities."

2:24 pm: "Our services continue to attract more customers, and both transacting and paid accounts reached new all-time highs in the quarter. We also have over one and a half billion paid subscriptions, which grew double digits during the quarter, reaching an all-time high."

2:26 pm: "Let's turn to our cash position and capital return program. We ended the quarter with $137 billion in cash and marketable securities and $80 billion in total debt. During the quarter, we returned $28 billion to shareholders. This included $3.9 billion in dividends and equivalents, and $24 billion in share repurchases."

2:26 pm: "We expect our December quarter total company revenue to grow between seven and 10% year over year, which reflects. which reflects our best view of constrained supply. We expect this to be the best quarter for revenue in the history of the company."

2:27 pm: "We expect services revenue to grow between eight and 9% year over year in the December quarter. This contemplates sequential headwinds, primarily driven by third-party licensing and foreign exchange. We expect gross margin to be between 45% and 46%. This includes primarily the impact of higher memory costs, as well as some costs related to the ramp of ‌Siri‌ AI."

2:27 pm: "We expect operating expenses to be between $20.4 billion and $20.8 billion. We expect OINE to be around $300 million, excluding any potential impact from the mark-to-market of minority investments, and our tax rate to be around 17 percent."

2:28 pm: John is introducing Apple COO Sabih Khan. "Many of you know Sabih from his work with worldwide operations and supply chain, leading many important functions at Apple, including manufacturing, AppleCare, environmental efforts, and supplier partnerships around the world. Sabih and his team are the reason we're able to build and deliver products at a scale and a and of a caliber unlike anyone else out there. I've asked Sabih to join Kevin and me on these calls as we take your questions."

2:29 pm: Q: On the iPhone 18, the standard model was left out of the September lineup. I was just wondering if you could share some of the reasons why, whether there were some supply constraints and component-related things that led to that decision, or if it had to do with the launch of the Duo, any color there would be helpful.

iPhone Duo and 18 Pro earlier this year in September, and we have iPhone 17, iPhone Air, and 17e continuing to kind of round out this incredibly strong lineup for the holidays. So obviously, we don't make any comments about future roadmap, but we're excited about where we're at.

2:31 pm: Q: My second question is just around iCloud+. It seems like it's becoming a more strategic product, just given the tie-in with home security as well as the potential monetization opportunity for Apple Intelligence. So I was just wondering, what are you seeing on ‌iCloud‌ Plus? Are there any tailwinds in terms of attach rates? You know, just particularly given the the rising cost for increased storage options on iPhone and the company's push into home products.

Apple TV and Apple Arcade in more than 100 countries and regions where we think we can really reach you know new potential subscribers, and then as you mentioned, you know we think there's good opportunities on ‌Apple Intelligence‌. You know there's going to be some usage limits on features that rely on server-side models, which include ‌Siri‌ AI and intelligent photo editing, some other things like that, and so anyone who needs greater capacity will be able to purchase expanded access in the future. So kind of to your point, in the beginning, ‌iCloud‌ tiers are largely about storage, but we've been you know adding more capabilities and features to it.

2:32 pm: Q: As the world of AI evolves from chatbots to consumer agents, it seems like there are growing opportunities for Apple. It also seems like there are risks. And John, I'd just love to get your perspective on what role you want Apple in ‌Siri‌ AI to play in kind of this consumer agentic AI landscape, and just how you look at any potential risks of some of these agents trying to encroach in your services. 

A: First and foremost we're incredibly excited to launch ‌Siri‌ AI alongside you know the the latest generation of ‌Apple Intelligence‌ features. ‌Siri‌ has long been popular with our users with more than two and a half billion requests every day, and with ‌Siri‌ AI we really have the kind of the ‌Siri‌ that we we always wanted. You know it's primarily request-based today, but as we talked about at WWDC, it's built on a modern orchestrator-driven architecture that gives us real room to expand its capabilities over time. As far as agentic capabilities, you know, we think these are promising tools for users. We just want to make sure that users are aware of what they're giving access to. We want to make sure this is done in a way that protects security and privacy. So, you know, we're pushing really hard on on that with ‌Siri‌ AI, but we're also really encouraged the fact that Apple devices we think are the best places to use all forms of AI.

2:35 pm: Q: How should we think about the durability of services growth. Just you know, I realized that was 10% in the September quarter. We're a little bit below that in the December quarter. You know, as certain things like search evolves and regulatory changes impact app store monetization, are there new services that we should be looking towards that you believe can become a more sizable offset to maybe take some pressure off these historically important revenue streams? 

App Store. And during the September quarter, the performance on the ‌App Store‌ was similar to the prior year, and we had a record number of paid subscriptions with double-digit growth for third-party apps on the ‌App Store‌. At the same time, we did see some headwinds in mobile gaming that we've talked about before, and expect to see those continue into the December quarter. And keep in mind, we also made some changes to the ‌App Store‌ business model in certain countries, and in the U.S. we continue to operate under a court ruling impacting the link out transactions.

As we move ahead, we expect services growth to to be between 8 to 9%, as I mentioned in the prepared remarks in the December quarter. And this outlook contemplates our best estimates on sequential headwinds, primarily from you know third-party licensing and the additional half percentage point of foreign exchange I just mentioned.

I think you know fundamentally we feel really good about the long-term opportunity that we have in our services business. You know we see continued growth in the install base of over 2.5 billion active devices, which is fundamentally the foundation for future growth, as more customers are able to experience our products and services. You know, example of this during the September quarter, ‌App Store‌ saw a record number of nearly a billion average weekly visitors, and we saw growth in the number of users who are paying for at least one service, reaching an all-time high. Another good example of this in India, we recently launched ‌Apple Pay‌ with Access Bank, bringing you know the seamless, safe, secure way to pay to one of the biggest markets in the world, and then on top of all this, as we talked about, we think you know intelligence is going to be another opportunity as well. So overall, we're feeling really good about about where we're headed in the long term.

2:37 pm: Q: You sort of described the iPhone as an intelligent personal hub in your opening comments, and you know, as personal AI agents become more prominent, do you see the potential for the primary customer relationship to shift from the device to the agent over time? And really, given Apple's integration of you know silicon hardware and software, where do you see the greatest opportunity to combine things like personal context and on-screen awareness into an agent that that can perhaps move beyond answering questions? And how far along do you think ‌Siri‌ is in bringing those pieces together right now?

A: We really do think of the the iPhone as the intelligent personal hub. I mean, if you think about it, so much of your personal data is on your iPhone. You know, whether it's your your contacts, your communications, health data, financial data, all of that, and ‌Siri‌ can tap into that and help you access it in a way that's very secure and private, and and that nobody else has access to. Even Apple doesn't have access to it, and so we think that is a a core kind of differentiator that that we're excited about, and we're going to continue to to push on that. And so I think this is an area that we feel really really good about.

2:40 pm: Q: The December quarter gross margin. I'm wondering if you'd spend a bit of time on that. I think if I exclude all the tariff refunds, you started implying gross margin would be down about 140 basis points sequentially, at least. Can you separate how much of this is maybe commodity memory inflation versus mix versus you called out ‌Siri‌ AI RAM costs as well? Can you just talk about what the different moving parts are as you think about the sequential.

A: We talked about a gross margin you know outlook between 45 and 46%. As you said, when you remove the benefit of the tariff free funds in September, the midpoint of the ranges it declined sequentially in the magnitude you mentioned. We expect most of that decline to be driven by higher memory costs.

Let me give you an overall view on memory. What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is is unprecedented, and as we said earlier in the September quarter, we did see higher memory costs as compared to the June quarter, which were partly offset by the benefit of carrying inventory and lower costs on certain non-memory components. Now, for the December quarter, we expect even higher memory costs, partly offset by a few factors. So, as you know, we changed the price on many of our products, including Mac and ‌iPad‌, at the end of June and iPhone in September, and these price increases provided some offset. We also expect to see some benefit from carry-in inventory in the December quarter as well, as well as lower costs on certain non-memory components. And looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase. As we said before, we do believe we'll see a decreasing benefit from the carry-in inventory on memory over time. 

And there's one more thing I wanted to add. As we work to improve supply, our manufacturing purchase obligations have increased by $33 billion from June to the September quarter, which you'll see in our annual filing when it comes out tomorrow.

As we continue to roll out ‌Siri‌ AI to more customers, the associated cloud costs will be recognized through services cost to sales. And consistent with how we've always accounted for Map, ‌Siri‌, and ‌iCloud‌ for the devices we sell that include these bundled services, we defer a portion of the revenue and recognize it over the life of the device. So, our hardware deferrals as of the December quarter will reflect the addition of ‌Siri‌ AI. Both of these items will have an impact to the gross margin. But as always, we you know we look to continue to make the investments necessary to support the business, and we also see a you know wide range of ways that AI can contribute to revenue growth over time. So on the product side, you know we feel AI offers a compelling reason for customers to upgrade and switch in order to get the latest capabilities, and we also feel those opportunities across third-party apps and partnerships as well as first-party opportunities, as John highlighted earlier, with the expanded access to you know server-side features of ‌Siri‌ AI and Apple intelligence features as well.

2:42 pm: Q: I wanted to ask you about your cash neutral policy. On one of the previous calls, you guys said that you weren't going to focus on that anymore, and that that that was not no longer the policy. What do you how under your leadership? What do you mean by that? Do you do you mean like you may go to net debt to buy back stock or do some M and A or go go the opposite way and hoard some cash again? Your thoughts on that would be welcome.

A: We did talk about the fact that we we're no longer using net cash neutral as a target. I think as we we explained on the last call or the last time we talked about that was the fact that we think it makes sense to evaluate our cash and debt position independently, and making sure we can optimize that and giving us the right flexibility. We remain committed to our capital allocation philosophy, which is we're going to invest everything we need to put in, you know, invest in our business and return excess cash to shareholders. And so we continue to maintain that discipline, and we do think this removal of net cash neutral just gives us flexibility to optimize so we can make the right investments with the company.

2:43 pm: Q: I realize you only guide one quarter at a time, but you know, from the 8 to 9%, when you think long term, I was wondering if you're willing to say you think whether it can accelerate from there and and whether AI could help you launch new services we haven't thought of yet that are accretive to the growth rate there.

A: I think you heard John talk about a lot of the long-term attributes that really you know feel give us optimism about the long-term opportunity in our services business. Again, we talked about things like the install base of over two and a half billion active devices. You know, we obviously saw you know a record number of weekly visitors in the ‌App Store‌ in September quarter. We also continue to see growth in users who are paying for at least a service, reaching all-time high in both, you know, transacting and paid accounts. We're excited about emerging markets. We talked about the launch of ‌Apple Pay‌ in India, but we continue to see good momentum in emerging markets in our services business, where we had double-digit growth. And so, we continue to feel really bullish about, you know, all the different elements as we as we look at the longer arc of time. And I think, as John mentioned, we are continuing to improve the features and reach of existing and new services as well. You know the example was the expansion of ‌iCloud‌ plans to include ‌Apple TV‌ and Arcade, obviously reaching you know you know a lot of new potential subscribers. ‌AppleCare‌ One Families another example of that. And so you know we continue to look for opportunities you know to grow our services business.

2:45 pm: Q: You're now competing for memory more so versus historically from pretty well capitalized companies who are signing long term agreements. So my question is: Is Apple changing anything in the way that you are procuring memory? How do you think about the progression of memory over time, and if it continues to be a headwind, is pricing also going to remain dynamic and potentially move higher?

A: We have worked with many of our suppliers for decades, and we deeply value their partnership over the years. We know our products would simply not be possible without them, and we look forward to continuing our work together. We're always working hard to improve supply, and as John said earlier, we our manufacturing purchase obligations have increased by $33 billion from the June to the September quarter. 

We're trying to manage through this with a number of actions. You were just talking about the fact we're continuing to pursue lower costs and non-memory components. John mentioned the fact that we have some benefit of care in inventory, and you know we did reluctantly make the decision to change pricing on a number of our products, right? Starting with the ‌iPad‌ and Mac in the June timeframe, and then iPhone more recently in September. I think what we try to do is evaluate and doing all that we evaluate the unit's revenue and margin, and we're really being thoughtful and deliberate at evaluating kind of the short term and long term considerations. And we really believe we're balancing this well.

2:46 pm: Q: It's the early days of launching this, can you give us some sense of how the token consumption associated with ‌Siri‌ AI is being done on-device versus private cloud compute versus GCP? And have you started to see any acceleration of usage? And if it does accelerate really fast globally, would it change your outlook on what you need to spend for compute?

A: We do envision, you know, ‌Siri‌ AI to kind of, you know, have queries that kind of are managed on device and also in the private cloud compute environment that we've outlined. The mix of that is still very early days, and so it's hard to predict exactly what the mix of those costs are going to look like. Obviously, on device, you know, it's very very efficient, no real costs associated with that. But on on the server side, you know, we would have some inference costs, and that's really the connection of the ‌Siri‌ AI related costs that I mentioned that would be you know recognized with services cost to sales. But I think again, we've just recently launched it and made it available to more users. And so in very very early stages of understanding the kind of mix of those costs, as well as any you know further requirements we might have on the compute side.

2:48 pm: Q: On the duo, can I just ask, in terms of maybe your thoughts in terms of or learnings from the launch of the duo and the demand that you've seen on that front, and what are the sort of supply chain related issues that you're facing right now that you probably need to iron out if you're trying to meet 
demand on that front? Any more visibility there in one when you reach supply demand balance?

A: We're thrilled with the initial response on the ‌iPhone Duo‌. ‌iPhone Duo‌ is constrained as of today. The ramp is going well, and we're working hard to get this revolutionary new product into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible. But at this time, it's really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance.

2:49 pm: Q: You have mentioned supply chain constraints impacting September quarter and going into December, but any way to sort of help us think about whether those are getting overall for the company, are those increasing in terms of magnitude relative to serve the impact on revenue? And if you are willing to sort of quantify those impacts for September and December?

A: During the September quarter, we experienced supply constraints on iPhone, Mac, and ‌iPad‌, and this was driven by the high levels of demand. And as we've said before, we're seeing less flexibility in the supply chain than normal. The Q4 constraints were primarily driven by the availability of the advanced nodes our SOCs are produced on, but as we've transitioned more of our line up to the latest two nanometer technology nodes, constraints on advanced nodes are easing.

For the December quarter, we expect constraints on Mac and ‌iPad‌, primarily driven by memory, as demand has been higher than what we expected.

2:50 pm: Q: I understand the memory price inflation. Kevin, it seems like it's probably like one to one and a half or two percentage points. Is this true and is there a availability issue with memory? Are you signing LTAs with memory suppliers so that availability not not an issue, even though pricing could still be an issue down the road? 

A: So as we said earlier, you know we are continuing to work to improve supply, and and you'll see that our manufacturing purchase obligations have increased by $33 billion from the June to the September quarter.

2:51 pm: Q: Any comments on the margin impact to think about going forward?

A: So when we look at the the margin change from the June quarter to the September quarter, and you remove the impact of the tariffs from both the June quarter and September quarter. We saw about a one-point sequential change in margin, and that was driven entirely by memory impacts. Now we did have some offsets because the gross memory impact was larger than that, but we had some offsets that John talked about earlier, driven by you know the benefit of care and inventory, some offsets from non-memory costs, as well as you know some of the benefits of pricing, and so as as we talked about, we expect the you know the memory costs to continue to you know be a challenge for us as we look in the December quarter, and our guide contemplates that right now. If you look at the the midpoint, most of this central decline we're expecting for the December quarter we expect to be driven by higher memory costs.

2:52 pm: Q: It seems like consumer AI agent space is seeing increasing competition with several app-based options. I'm just wondering, you know, when you look at the agent capability of ‌Siri‌ built into the OS class platform versus AI agents that are confined within an app architecture. How do you see that evolving?

A: ‌Siri‌ right now is primarily request-based, and as we talked about before, it is built on a modern orchestrator-driven architecture. So we see you know opportunity to expand its capabilities over time. We think fundamentally, you know what's most important to us is that we're giving people these capabilities that are private and secure, and we're really focused on protecting people's data.

2:53 pm: Q: Can you help us understand sort of the difference or maybe the delta of quantity versus price across sort of the product lineup? Because it certainly looks like you know you're looking at double digit growth across the iPhone and the Mac business, and we all know I think in the industry that there's been pretty strong price inflation across the PC Mac ecosystem and. And you guys mentioned that you've reluctantly taken price as well. So can you help us understand kind of what's the driving dynamics in that market? 

A: We don't normally provide that level of detail or color as we look at the outlook, other than to say, again, we we did guide to the 7 to 10% year on year, and again, just as a reminder, that is on top of a phenomenal December quarter last year, where revenue grew 16%. And so, you know, we don't provide the level of detail, but I would say it's early to really read price elasticity at this point in time. You know, the ‌iPad‌ and Mac were constrained since you know kind of we made those adjustments, and again, we just recently. recently just adjusted the price on iPhone, so it's really early to really assess any elasticity impact at this stage.

2:54 pm: Q: Going back to the investment cycle, whether it's agentic, Siri-related, you know, it looks like you guys had you're coming off of a year of you know very aggressive investments in R & D to you know to fund the business going forward and to grow the business. You know, if I just think about kind of the commentary on Q1 of fiscal 27, certainly sounds like that spending is moderating a little bit. Can you maybe walk through some of the puts and takes in terms of what's driving that moderation in spend across the operating line items? 

A: Here we don't break out you know, detail on our outlook, but but I would you know reiterate the fact that for the December quarter, we do expect OpEx to grow between 11 and 13 percent year over year, which is driven by increased you know and continued investment in R&D, in particular AI. This growth rate is coming down, as you alluded from the levels of growth we had in FY '26. But you know, as we said before, we continue to significantly increase our overall investments in AI while continue to invest. in the product roadmap, and you know our December guide is a continued reflection of that. We feel confident that we're in spending what we need to spend to achieve our roadmap.

2:56 pm: Q: Your latest MacBook Pros included more iOS features like Touch and Dynamic Island, as well as obviously ‌Siri‌ AI. Should we anticipate further close linking of macOS and iOS features? Maybe even pointing at some point to a single unified OS, either for simplicity or to reduce costs?

A: We are very proud of both the Mac and the ‌iPad‌, and and I think what you've seen over the years is we've really enjoyed the ability to bring features and capabilities across the ecosystem and and create you know really compelling features that span you know things between handoff between iPhone and Mac and ‌iPad‌. And so when we when we design the product, we're looking at how can we make the best version of each and every product. And if you look at what we just did last week with the ‌MacBook Pro‌, we took a huge leap forward. These these MacBook Pros are better in every way than the the ones that came before them, and we're really proud of that. And so we don't we don't have any fundamentally different changes that we're planning right now. Nor would we talk about it anyway.

2:57 pm: Q: We saw two years of declines in China sales, and then this year, Apple obviously grew a very healthy 28% in FY 26. Can you talk through to what you attribute that recovery, and whether you think Greater China can sustain these sort of elevated levels of growth, which are really leading the company regionally now?

A: Let me give you some color on China. We were very pleased with the performance in Greater China. Right, revenue was up 21% during the September quarter, which was a quarterly record. The performance was primarily driven by iPhone, where we set a September quarter record, and by Mac, where we saw very strong double-digit growth. And taking a step back, Greater China was up 28% for the full year. You know, Tim and Sabih were just in China meeting with customers and developers and partners, and it has been wonderful to see the customer reaction to our latest lineup of products, including ‌iPhone Duo‌. Our installed base of active devices has reached an all-time high, and we had a record year for iPhone upgraders in mainland China. According to a survey from World Panel, iPhone models were the top three selling smartphones in urban China, and we think we gained share on iPhone and Mac.

MacBook Air and ‌MacBook Neo‌ were the top two selling laptop models, and Mac Mini was the top selling desktop model in the September quarter. So I guess to answer your question, we think the success comes from having really great products.

2:59 pm: Q: I'm interested in your thoughts with higher device prices. How you think about the environment around affordability programs and the importance to to volumes with respect to trade-ins, subsidies, and other options. And you know what Apple can do to encourage more of that independently of funding it yourself?

A: When we're building products and then when we're pricing them, we're always focused on you know building the best products and services in the world and delivering incredible value to our customers. Obviously, as we talked about, you know, these these memory prices are unprecedented, and so that has put pressure on our prices. But it's been great to see the success of the products, and you know, we have been investing in programs like the Apple Upgrade Program, which is a great way to help affordability, and so. And so these afford affordability programs are definitely an important important factor.

2:59 pm: The call is complete.

title: High-end robotic ‘HomeView Ultra’ could land in 2028 for $1,000
content:
Macworld





While we all wait for Apple’s HomeView smart home hub to ship, we’re reminded that Apple has been working on a larger, robotic version of the same thing for years. A new report from The Information shares some details about the so-called “HomeView Ultra” (which has reportedly been floated but may or may not launch under that name).
According to the report, this larger HomeView would have a roughly 9-inch display, giving it about 65 percent more screen area than the 7-inch display on the HomeView. It would be attached to its base via a robotic arm that somewhat resembles the iMac G4 or the Pixar lamp. It would feature cameras and sensors that make it aware of its environment, so it can do things like follow you around during a FaceTime call, turn on lights when someone enters a room, or even shoo the cat off the table.
Apple published a research paper last year showing an R&D project for a robotic lamp with personality, and it’s enough to make you instantly want one. If the robotic HomeView similarly animates and moves as though it has a soul, it might even justify the estimated $1,000 price tag.
The report claims that the device, code-named J595, will ship later next year at the earliest, or perhaps in 2028. Most telling is that the hardware has apparently been more or less complete for two years, but is waiting on the software to catch up. Also, there has apparently been some debate about which features should be in the 1st-generation device and which should wait for the 2nd-gen model. According to The Information, the autonomous AI features are ambitious and not ready yet, so the release timing is all about balancing the AI development with the first-generation feature set.

title: Don’t worry, full-sized iPad fans, the model you want is getting an update soon
content:
Macworld





The announcement of the 8th-gen iPad mini last week included several major improvements on the previous model: a thinner and lighter design, a larger and brighter screen, dust and water resistance, and a big processor upgrade. As is often the case with Apple’s disjointed and confusing iPad range, however, this isolated update leaves the rest of the company’s tablets looking rather out of date.
As the lineup currrenty stands, the baseline iPad has an A16, a full four chip generations behind the mini’s A20 Pro. It can’t run Apple Intelligence or Siri AI and looks thoroughly underpowered. The current iPad Air, meanwhile, costs $50 more than the mini but misses out on the latter’s OLED screen (and nano-texture finish), fast-charge capabilities, and new Acoustic Display feature… plus it’s nowhere near as slim. And the iPad Pro still has an M5 despite the M6 arriving for the MacBook and Mac mini.
But there’s good news for prospective iPad customers, because those older models are reportedly headed towards their own refresh early next year. In the latest edition of his Power On newsletter, Bloomberg reporter Mark Gurman predicts that Apple “will turn its attention to a slew of other tablet updates in 2027,” going on to specify that these updates will likely happen in the first half of the year.
This means imminent new versions of all three non-mini iPad lines. Gurman offers little detail about the next edition of the baseline iPad, other than to note that recent price hikes have put it well above previously comparable rivals. To justify the pricing, one would imagine a significant boost to the device’s processing muscle is required, which would align with the most recent rumors. 
Gurman is more illuminating on the subject of the next iPad Air, which he expects to switch to OLED in order to match the iPad mini. That would presumably come with a $100 price hike as well, which would put some space between it and the iPad mini.
The most compelling update, perhaps inevitably, will be the “faster” next generation of iPad Pro at the top of the range. “The big change on the high-end machine is likely to be the addition of a vapor chamber to cool things down during gaming and intensive AI tasks,” Gurman writes. The vapor chamber was one of the headline updates in the iPhone 17 Pro last year. The idea that it will make the move to the iPad Pro is a rumor, we should add, that’s been making the rounds since at least 2025.
It isn’t clear how Apple plans to unveil the new iPads. The company has been known to hold a press event in the spring, with the last such event being held in May 2024 to announce the M4 iPad Pro. A reveal at WWDC 2027, which will take place in June, would technically count as the first half of the year, but WWDC usually focuses on software with minimal hardware discussion. Based on the events of last month, however, it may be more likely for Apple to announce the new models via smaller “experiences,” press releases, and quiet updates to its website.

title: Best MacBook for 2026: Air vs Pro vs Neo compared
content:
Macworld





Apple sells several MacBook models across different sizes, prices, and performance levels, so choosing the right one depends on your budget, the type of work you do, and how much power you actually need.
In this in-depth guide, we explain which MacBook is best for different users, compare the latest MacBook Air, MacBook Neo and the MacBook Pro models (with and without touchscreen), and help you decide how much RAM and how much storage you really need.
Choosing a MacBook Pro now involves two decisions: how much processing power you need, and which display you want. The entry-level 14-inch model uses the M6 chip, while more demanding users can choose M5 Pro or M5 Max configurations with either a non-touch Liquid Retina XDR display or a PROLED XDR OLED touchscreen.
For most people, the MacBook Air remains our recommended starting point. If you need a Pro, choose the chip, memory and storage around your workload, then consider whether the touchscreen model’s OLED display and lighter design justify the extra cost. In this article, we’ll help you decide whether a MacBook Air, MacBook Pro, or MacBook Neo is the best fit for your needs.


Which MacBook is right for you?
In 2026, Apple’s laptop lineup spans five main choices: the budget-friendly MacBook Neo, the mainstream MacBook Air, the M6 MacBook Pro, the high-performance M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro and the touchscreen versions of those MacBook Pro models.
Best for basic use and tight budgets: MacBook Neo is ideal for students, casual browsing, streaming, and light productivity at the lowest entry price.
Best for most people: MacBook Air (M5)  offers the best mix of portability, battery life, silent operation, and everyday performance.
Best for those who want a superior display and extra ports: The MacBook Pro (M6) offers professional-grade features without the extreme power of the M5 Pro or M5 Max chips. 
Best for professionals and power users: MacBook Pro (M5 Pro/Max) is best for demanding workflows such as 4K video editing, 3D work, heavy multitasking, and software development.
Best for high-end creative professionals: Suited to those who work extensively on their laptop’s built-in display and need direct touch interaction. 
Use the table below to quickly find the MacBook that best suit your needs, or read on for more detailed guide to help you choose the best MacBook for your specific needs.

The MacBook Air (M5) is the best MacBook for most buyers because it offers the strongest balance of price, portability, battery life, and performance.
The 13-inch MacBook Air is light, quiet, fast enough for everyday work, and easier to recommend than any other Mac laptop. The latest version, updated in March 2026, keeps the same winning formula while improving storage and connectivity. There is also a 15-inch version for anyone who wants a larger screen. 
What’s new
The latest MacBook Air features the M5 chip, base storage is 512GB, and it supports newer wireless standards including Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.
Why we recommend the MacBook Air
Excellent balance of performance and portability
Silent fanless design
Long battery life
Strong everyday performance for work, school, and travel
Now ships with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage as standard
Sizes
The MacBook Air comes in two sizes:
13-inch MacBook Air, 13.6-inch screen: Best for portability
15-inch MacBook Air, 15.3-inch screen: Better for multitasking and split-screen work
Display
As you can see from the above measurements, the display, when measured diagonally is a little larger than the standard naming would suggest. As a result the 13-inch MacBook Air display is actually larger than that on the 13-inch MacBook Neo, discussed below. The MacBook Air uses a bright Liquid Retina display, but it still lacks the 120Hz ProMotion refresh rate and HDR capabilities found on MacBook Pro models.
Performance
The M5 chip in the MacBook Air is fast enough for office work, school tasks, web apps, multitasking, and light creative work. Because the Air has no fan, though, performance can dip during long video exports or other sustained heavy workloads so that the temperature remains optimal.
Battery life
Battery life is excellent, making the Air a great choice for anyone who works away from a desk. It offers more battery life than the budget-friendly MacBook Neo, but falls short of the 14-inch MacBook Pro. 
Other specs
You get MagSafe 3 for charging and two Thunderbolt 4 ports. The MacBook Air also supports up to two external displays. (Older M1 and M2 models were limited to one external monitor). 
16GB RAM to 32GB RAM
From 512GB to 4TB SSD
Price
Apple put MacBook Air prices up by $200 in June 2026. 
13-inch MacBook Air: Now starts at $1,299/£1,299

What to know before buying
The Air’s biggest limitation is sustained performance. It is quick for most tasks, but it is not the right machine for users who regularly push their system for long periods. The MacBook Air is likely to soon adopt the M6 chip as used in the entry-level MacBook Pro, Mac mini and iMac.

MacBook Air vs MacBook Pro: Which should you buy?

				
					

				
			
The M5 MacBook Air and M6 MacBook Pro are different in some significant ways.

Foundry




The MacBook Air is our recommendation for most people, offering enough performance for everyday work and light creative projects in a thin, light, silent design. Choose the MacBook Pro if you regularly run demanding workloads or will benefit from its better display and additional ports.
The closest comparison is between the M5 MacBook Air and 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro. For more demanding professional work, the MacBook Pro also offers M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, with a choice of non-touchscreen or PROLED XDR touchscreen displays.
Performance: Do you need a MacBook Pro?
The M5 MacBook Air is well suited to web browsing, office apps, studying, photo editing, and occasional video projects. Using creative software doesn’t automatically mean you need a Pro: the size of your projects and how frequently you run demanding tasks matter more.
The M6 MacBook Pro combines a newer chip generation with active cooling. Its fans help it sustain performance during lengthy video exports, code compilation, and other intensive tasks. The Air’s fanless design keeps it completely silent, but performance can fall during prolonged heavy workloads.
If these demanding tasks make up much of your working day, consider an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro. These offer greater processing, graphics, and memory capacity than the standard M6 model. A newer chip generation doesn’t automatically make the M6 the more powerful choice.
Display and ports: What does the Pro add?
The MacBook Air’s Liquid Retina display is suitable for everyday work, with 500 nits brightness and a 60Hz refresh rate. You can choose a 13-inch model for portability or a 15-inch model for more workspace.
The M6 MacBook Pro’s 14.2-inch Liquid Retina XDR display adds mini-LED technology, deeper contrast, brighter HDR highlights, and ProMotion adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. These features are particularly useful for viewing and editing HDR content, although you don’t need to be a creative professional to appreciate the screen.
The M6 Pro also provides three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, and an SDXC card slot. The Air has two Thunderbolt 4 ports, so connecting memory cards, HDMI displays, or several accessories may require adapters or a dock.
For an OLED touchscreen, choose a PROLED XDR MacBook Pro with an M5 Pro or M5 Max chip. Touchscreen availability is a separate consideration from how much processing power you need.
Portability, battery life, and price
The Air is thinner and lighter, making it the stronger choice if you carry your laptop regularly. The 15-inch Air is also worth considering if you want a larger screen without the weight and expense of a 16-inch Pro.
The M6 MacBook Pro has a higher advertised battery-life rating, although actual endurance depends on your workload. Both models are suitable for working away from a power socket.
The Air costs less, but compare configurations with matching memory and storage before deciding. The M6 Pro starts with more storage, which narrows the price difference if you would otherwise upgrade the Air.
Our buying advice: Air or Pro?
Buy the MacBook Air for everyday work, studying, travel, and light creative projects. It offers the best balance of performance, portability, and price for most buyers.
Buy the M6 MacBook Pro if you want its HDR display, additional ports, longer advertised battery life, or better sustained performance.
Choose an M5 Pro or M5 Max MacBook Pro for demanding professional workloads that justify more processing power, graphics performance, or memory. Consider the PROLED XDR version if you also want OLED and touch.
