 FAQ 


1.
Which MacBook lasts the longest?
For battery life, the MacBook Pro models lead the lineup, with 24 hours of playback.





2.
Should I buy a refurbished MacBook?
A refurbished MacBook can be a good value, especially if you buy Apple silicon rather than Intel. Just make sure the price gap is meaningful and the machine still has enough life left to justify the purchase.
Since Apple put up prices across the range buying in the Refurbished Store is even more attractive. The MacBook Air, MacBook Neo and MacBook Pro were all available at the original price shortly after Apple raised prices. 
For example, the MacBook Neo is $599, you can get a 13-inch, M5 MacBook Air for $1,099 and a 14-inch MacBook Pro, M5 Pro for $2,119.





3.
Is a MacBook Air powerful enough?
Yes. For most people, the MacBook Air is more than powerful enough for everyday work, school, multitasking, web use, and light creative tasks.





4.
Is a MacBook worth it compared to a Windows laptop?
That depends on your priorities, but MacBooks are often worth the extra cost if you value exceptional battery life, premium build quality, class-leading trackpads, and seamless integration with the Apple ecosystem.
Apple’s recent price increases have made Macs more expensive, but the company isn’t alone in raising prices. Lenovo also announced price rises in June 2026, while other PC manufacturers have warned that soaring memory and storage costs are putting pressure on margins, making higher prices increasingly likely across the industry. As a result, the price gap between Macs and comparable Windows laptops may not be as large as it first appears.





5.
How long will a MacBook last?
The typical lifespan of a MacBook is generally between five and eight years, though this depends heavily on a combination of hardware durability and ongoing software support . While the physical components are built to last, Apple eventually classifies older models as “vintage” or “obsolete,” which limits your ability to get official repairs and parts. Find out more here: How long do MacBooks last: Lifespan, support and when to upgrade.

title: Apple’s probably done announcing new hardware, but November is still pretty jammed
content:
Macworld





Apple should finally be done announcing new hardware for 2026, but there’s still plenty to be released this month. We’ve got the new MacBook Pro with PROLED, M6 iMac, M6 MacBook Pro, HomeView, and Apple TV 4K that were all announced in October.
There’s some exciting software, too. We expect the OS 27.3 updates to bring more new features, including Audio Intelligence to the Apple Watch series 12 and Ultra 4, as well and the new Health app and perhaps a few other new capabilities. And naturally, we’ll get new Apple TV+ shows and Apple Arcade games, as we do every month. Here’s what we can expect from Apple in November 2026.
New hardware
Apple isn’t expected to announce any new hardware in November, but a lot of the products announced in October don’t actually ship until this month. Here’s what we have on the way.
MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display: The new tandem-OLED MacBook Pro with touch support and the Dynamic Island is shipping on November 6.
M6 iMac: Apple finally updated the iMac with a new processor, though nothing else has changed. It ships on November 6 as well.
iPad mini with OLED: The new iPad mini gets a big upgrade, with an OLED display and an A20 Pro processor. It arrives on November 6, too.
HomeView: Announced last month, the HomeView is the first truly new-category product from Apple in a long time. It doesn’t ship until November 13, so there haven’t even been any reviews yet.
Apple TV 4K (4th gen): The new Apple TV 4K box has a faster processor for Siri AI, built-in microphones, and a remote that has a speaker for Find My. It arrives on November 13.
Apps and software updates
We all get excited about new hardware, but new software updates impact over a billion users and, sometimes, all the cool new stuff is just software that comes to your existing devices. Apple released the OS 27.2 updates at the end of October, which brought several new features.
OS 27.3: Apple’s big OS 27 software updates aren’t done yet—there are still a few significant features to come. Among them are a new redesigned Health app, further enhancements to Siri AI, support for Siri AI on HomePod mini and existing Apple TV 4K boxes.
We expect the OS 27.3 beta to begin in the first week of November, with the final release likely arriving in late November or early December.
Services
Apple TV+
Here are the shows, series, and movies we expect to release on Apple TV+ in November 2026. If you want to know what’s coming later, check our full guide to upcoming Apple TV+ content.
Stick (season 2): A sports comedy about a washed-up ex-pro golfer who coaches a young 17-year-old phenom. November 4
Awkwafina: The Unlikely Cook: Hollywood actor and comedian Nora Lum (aka Awkwafina) is the descendant of restaurant royalty … but she can’t cook. Join the star on an inspiring culinary road trip as she learns the craft and attempts to revive her family’s beloved Chinese eatery. November 6
12 12 12: Each episode of 12 12 12 unfolds across three timelines of a heist: the 12 months of planning, the 12 hours of the heist, and the 12 days following. November 13 (Get it?)
Being Heumann: In 1977, young disabled Judy Heumann and a scrappy coalition of outsiders decide they’ve had enough. What begins as one impulsive act becomes the longest occupation of a federal building in American history, as hundreds spontaneously seize government offices and refuse to leave until the bureaucrat in their way takes action. November 13
Way of the Warrior Kid: Middle school has been a nightmare for Marc, a good kid who’s bullied by his classmates and feels like he’s behind in everything, from academics to P.E. to just making friends. That changes when his injured Uncle Jake, a decorated Navy SEAL, comes to spend the summer and recuperate with Marc and his mom, Sarah. November 25
Apple Arcade
Apple releases most Apple Arcade games in the first week of each month. Check our Apple Arcade FAQ for a full list of Apple Arcade games and more details on the service. Occasionally, games are released with no forewarning, but you’ll usually see next month’s releases listed in the Coming Soon section.
Crossy Road Rush: A platforming island endless runner in the Crossy Road cinematic universe. November 5
Food Stylist – Design Game+: A cozy design game about plating fancy food and making it look great. November 5
KAMI 2+: A calm, color-and-shape logic puzzle game. November 5

title: Apple Isn't Done With 2026: Here's What's Still Coming
content:
Apple's busiest season isn't over yet. Far from it. With two hardware launch dates still to come in November, plus software updates and new smart home accessories running into December, there's more on the way from Apple before the end of 2026, so be sure to stick around.


Below, we've rounded up what's still coming, along with one date in particular that's worth watching if you're a holiday shopper.


Apple Intelligence testing in China – November 4: The first Apple Intelligence features for users in China enter testing in the latest iOS developer beta from Wednesday, November 4. Apple has partnered with Alibaba to add Qwen support to Siri, Writing Tools, and Visual Intelligence.

Five new products – November 6: Apple is launching five products this Friday: the OLED iPad mini with A20 Pro (from $699), the M6 iMac (from $1,499), the 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6 (from $1,999), and all-new 14-inch and 16-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌ models with ‌OLED‌ touchscreens (from $2,899 and $3,399). The latter two are Apple's first touchscreen Macs. Pre-orders are already open, but individual delivery dates vary based on region and configuration.

Apple HomeView – November 13: Apple's new smart home display arrives on Friday, November 13, priced at $299. Available in tabletop and wall-mounted versions, the hub can be used to answer questions with ‌Siri‌ AI, display pictures, make FaceTime calls, play music, show recipes, offer up calendar events, and more. Pre-orders are already open in launch markets, but HomeView will not initially be sold in the European Union.

Apple TV 4K – November 13: The fourth-generation Apple TV 4K launches alongside HomeView, and is also priced at $299. Unlike previous generations, there's just the one model with 128GB storage, and it adds ‌Siri‌ AI and supports four-speaker surround sound with HomePod mini 2 or second-generation HomePod speakers. Pre-orders are already open.

Apple Creator Studio updates – November: Updates coming this month bring built-in MotionVFX content to Final Cut Pro, Generate Fill to Pixelmator Pro, and new AI assistants in beta to Logic Pro, Keynote, Pages, and Numbers. The updates are free for existing subscribers.

Black Friday – November 27: It's not a product launch, but a date likely worth marking. Apple has held a four-day shopping event over the Black Friday weekend in recent years, when it has typically offered gift cards with eligible purchases. Our Black Friday roundup will be tracking the deals.

iOS 27.3 and Apple Intelligence in China – December: Apple has confirmed the public rollout of its first ‌Apple Intelligence‌ features in China for December, alongside iOS 27.3. The initial release is for supported iPhones, with other platforms to follow after the required regulatory approvals.

Apple Home Collection – from December: The new Apple-backed, third-party lineup includes smart home cameras, thermostats, and a lock designed with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. Apple says that availability begins in December, although select accessories will not arrive until early 2027.

title: Apple 'HomeView Ultra' With 9-Inch 360º Screen Detailed in New Report
content:
The Information's Aaron Tilley today reported that Apple has been developing a larger, robotic version of the HomeView. This device has been called a "HomeView Ultra" or "HomeView Max" in rumors, but the final name might be different.


Tilley said a prototype of the device is equipped with a 9-inch display on a swiveling arm, with its overall design said to look similar to Apple's old iMac G4 or Pixar's lamp mascot. Like the HomeView, the device would have standard features like FaceTime, but it would also be "fully aware of its environment and act autonomously."

"The current design for the robot envisions it using a camera and sensors to be fully aware of its environment and act autonomously, allowing it to turn on the lights when someone walks into a room—or perhaps even try to tell a cat to get off a table," the report said. "It is meant to be smart enough to avoid accidentally hitting objects around it."

The report said the device's hardware has largely been finalized for around two years, but there have apparently been "internal disagreements" within Apple, particularly in regards to which software features should be available on the first-generation model or postponed until a second-generation model already being discussed.

The report said Apple is hoping to release the larger HomeView in 2027 for around $1,000 in the U.S., but the device might not be ready to launch until 2028.

Apple has also explored other types of robots, such as one that follows a user around the home on wheels, one that flies inside the home, and one that can fold clothes, but it is unclear if any of these devices will ever be released.

title: Best USB-C hubs and adapters for Mac 2026

Macworld





USB-C and its Thunderbolt variant are the most up-to-date standards of the USB connector. They allow data-transfer speeds of up to 80Gbps, can fast-charge devices up to 240W, and conveniently fit in a port either way up—which means that you can wave bye-bye to the age-old USB guessing game of “Which way does it go in?”.
USB-C is no one-trick pony—handling data transfer, video output and power input. You’ll find faster variants of USB-C (called Thunderbolt 3, 4 or 5) on Macs. Each version of Thunderbolt is backwards compatible with USB-C so the adapters reviewed here will all work with modern Macs—from the MacBooks Neo, Air and Pro, through to the desktop iMac, Mac mini and Studio. USB-C’s 5-10Gbps speeds will limit some of Thunderbolt’s more impressive 40 to 80Gbps potential but for most people even 5Gbps is fast enough. If super-fast data transfer is one of your requirements, a number of hubs reviewed below do use Thunderbolt or 40Gbps USB4. Find out more in our Thunderbolt 5 vs Thunderbolt 4 vs Thunderbolt 3 comparison and also our chart at the end showing all the ports of Apple’s recent Macs.

				
					

				
			
Apple




In general, an “adapter” works with a single port (such as USB-A or Ethernet) while a “hub” gives you multiple ports. If you require even more, then look for a “docking station” or “dock“. Docks usually come with their own power supply, while hubs require a separate USB-C charger if you need a power source. If you’re after a full desktop setup for your MacBook, look out for our recommendations for the best USB-C and Thunderbolt docking stations for MacBooks.
Apple sells its own range of USB-C adapters to HDMI, VGA and more, but they are overpriced and underpowered compared to the premium USB-C hubs and adapters we have reviewed here. We haven’t included the many much cheaper but lower-quality versions you can find online as we recommend only from trusted and tested makers. There are plenty of affordable solutions tested and reviewed here that are of a higher quality.
Look for each hub’s video capability for connecting to external displays. Most support only one monitor, but some offer two—note that more than two usually requires an extra software install.
Passthrough power will likely also be of interest to MacBook users. 60W Power Delivery (PD) will work even for the 16-inch MacBook Pro (just), but more watts equals a faster charge.
Note that the ports on the MacBook Neo are USB-C and only one of them is properly data-ready at 10Gbps, with the other just for charging. Read more on how the MacBook Neo’s USB-C ports are different. As it has just one data port, a USB-C hub becomes a must for expanding the Neo’s potential—read our roundup of the best MacBook Neo accessories.
Below the list of our favorite USB hubs and adapters, we describe the types of ports you might require from a hub and what to look for in each.

This adapter is designed to help owners of really quite old Macs smoothly transition to using USB-C. You may well have devices such as hard drives and external displays that use Thunderbolt 2 connections. This little gadget lets you keep using them with your MacBook or new MacBook Pro.
It also allows new Thunderbolt 3, 4 and 5 devices to connect to a Mac with Thunderbolt 2 ports–but to take advantage of it this way round Apple advises you need to be running macOS Sierra or above.

							
		
Which extra ports do you need in a hub
Many MacBook users connect their laptop to one or more external displays for greater screen space. You can connect to monitors using USB-C (via adapters to non-USB-C monitors) or better a dedicated video port, such as HDMI or DisplayPort. Check the hub specs to see which displays they support: some are limited to HD displays, others support 4K (also known as UHD) displays. The refresh rate is also important. 4K at 30Hz is fine for most productivity and browsing tasks, but watching video or playing games demands higher refresh rates of at least 60Hz.
You may need some legacy non-reversible USB-A ports, and most adapters and hubs have at least one for your non-USB-C memory sticks and drives. Look for at least USB 3.0, which has a speedy bandwidth of 5Gbps compared to the lamentably sluggish USB 2.0’s 480Mbps.
To fast-charge an iPhone, you need a minimum of 18W and it has to be USB-C, so look for extra USB-C slots with charging power, which are more capable than USB-A.
Other ports to look for in a hub include Ethernet for faster wired Internet access (without the flakiness of Wi-Fi). You can choose from standard Gigabit Ethernet (1000Mbps) or 2.5Gb and even 5Gb and 10Gb Ethernet (2500-10000Mbps), although the faster Ethernet requires the whole network to support that speed.
An SD or microSD card reader is perfect for adding inexpensive portable storage to your system. Card readers come at different speeds: UHS-I at 104MBps, and UHS-II at 312MBps; although some are slower at 60MBps.
Look for hubs that offer passthrough charging, so you can charge your laptop even though you are using up one of the laptop’s USB-C ports for the hub itself. Most don’t ship with a charger, so you’ll need to add your own, and remember that it needs to be a 100W charger to give 85W and above charging if offered by the hub. Lower wattage chargers are fine but will limit the hub’s charging potential. Couple your hub with one of the best Mac USB-C chargers. See how much power your MacBook needs in our advice below the list of recommended hubs and adapters.
You can also buy USB-C adapters for the many older display standards out there, such as VGA and DVI. We’ve picked the best for you below.
Many hubs and docks aren’t compatible with Apple’s SuperDrive CD/DVD drive. We’ve found few dock makers that offers compatibility with the SuperDrive, the Caldigit Thunderbolt Element Hub and OWC Thunderbolt Dock being two that do.
Which ports does each Mac have?
Here are the onboard ports on all of Apple’s current and recent Macs:
MacBook Neo: 2x USB-C (one for 10Gbps data and one for charging), 3.5mm headphone jack
MacBook Air: 2x Thunderbolt 4, MagSafe 3 charging port, 3.5mm headphone jack
MacBook Pro (plain M4/M5/M6): 3x Thunderbolt 4, MagSafe 3 charging port, HDMI, SDXC Card Reader (250MBps), 3.5mm headphone jack
MacBook Pro (M4/M5 Pro/Max): 3x Thunderbolt 5, MagSafe 3 charging port, HDMI, SDXC Card Reader (250MBps), 3.5mm headphone jack
iMac (24-inch): 2x Thunderbolt 4/USB4 or 4x Thunderbolt 4, 3.5mm headphone jack, optional Gigabit Ethernet
Mac mini M4/M6: 3x Thunderbolt 4, 2x USB-C (10Gbps), HDMI, Gigabit Ethernet, 3.5mm headphone jack
Mac mini M4 Pro: 3x Thunderbolt 5, 2x USB-C (10Gbps), HDMI, Gigabit Ethernet, 3.5mm headphone jack
Mac mini M5 Pro: 3x Thunderbolt 5, 2x USB-C (10Gbps), HDMI, 2.5Gb Ethernet, 3.5mm headphone jack
Mac Studio M4 Pro, M5 Max: 4x Thunderbolt 5, 2x USB-C (10Gbps), 2x USB-A (5Gbps), HDMI, 10Gb Ethernet, SDXC Card Reader (312MBps), 3.5mm headphone jack
Mac Studio M3/M5 Ultra: 6x Thunderbolt 5, 2x USB-A (5Gbps), HDMI, 10Gb Ethernet, SDXC Card Reader (312MBps), 3.5mm headphone jack
Mirrored or Extended Modes for Mac displays
When you attach more than one external display to a Mac you can choose between various setups. Most hubs with more than one video port—usually HDMI—can mirror your MacBook’s screen, but most can at best handle showing a different screen to the Mac but not different to each other when attempting Extended Mode.
For full extended Mode, where each of the screens shows a different image and you treat each as an extension to your workspace—moving your cursor and windows easily between the displays—you will likely need a hub or dock that supports free third-party DisplayLink software, which is easy to download and install. Included above are reviews of the Plugable Dual and Quad HDMI adapters, both of which work with DisplayLink. DisplayLink enables multiple screens even with plain M1 and M2 MacBooks that are technically limited to just one external display.
If you need even more ports than you’ll find on a hub, check our reviews of the best DisplayLink docks.

				
					

				
			
Baseus




How much power does each MacBook require for smooth running
Check the Power Delivery (PD) charging power each hub or adapter offers connected laptops or iPads. 
The MacBook Neo charges at 20W.
The 13-inch MacBook Air charges at 30W, but can fast-charge at 70W and above.
The 13-inch MacBook Pro and 15-inch MacBook Air charge at 70W for fast charging, but even 45W would keep you topped up if running basic tasks at the time. Apple recommends at least 60W for the 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro.
The higher-end 14-inch (M3/M4/M5/M6, M4/M5 Pro/Max) and 16-inch MacBook Pro require at least 96W for fast charging, but can cope at 60W or 70W. The 16-inch MacBook Pro prefers 140W, but is fine with 94W unless under extreme processing tasks.
You can certainly use a charger at lower power, but remember that it will power up slower than when using a higher-wattage charger, and if too low your laptop might run out of juice altogether when maxed out on power-hungry apps and devices. And you can use a higher-power charger without any concerns. The device being charged decides how much power it requires.

title: Hundreds of AI apps were part of a network hiding sexually abusive deepfake tools
content:
Apple has removed 19 apps that concealed sexually abusive AI deepfake tools behind ordinary features after an investigation uncovered a network designed to evade App Store review.

App Store
A November 2 investigation identified more than 400 connected apps and web domains that appeared to offer harmless AI services, including pet portraits, language lessons, and fitness coaching. Some could instead load tools for generating sexually explicit images and videos using photographs of real people.
The findings build on earlier research showing that apps capable of creating nonconsensual sexual imagery were reaching the App Store despite Apple's restrictions. The newly uncovered network went further by using remote servers to control which features appeared to individual users.

title: It's not clear if macOS Golden Gate really did anything for ultrawide monitors
content:
Apple says that macOS Golden Gate greatly improves ultrawide monitor support, Reddit says it doesn't, and an AppleInsider staffer simply can't tell.


Apple claims to have improved ultrawide monitor support in macOS Golden Gate. Background monitor image credit: Samsung.

title: Canva Brings Free All-in-One Affinity App to iPad
content:
Canva today released Affinity for iPad, bringing its free all-in-one design app to Apple's tablet, along with a new Sketch Studio built for touch and Apple Pencil.


The release follows last year's desktop app relaunch, which combined the previously separate Affinity Designer, Photo, and Publisher apps into a single app for Mac and Windows. Canva had promised an iPad version in 2026, and says the desktop app has since attracted more than seven million sign-ups.

The iPad app brings sketching, vector graphics, photo editing, and page layout together in one interface. Users can switch between Sketch, Vector, Pixel, and Layout studios while working in the same .af file, which can also be opened on desktop.

Sketch Studio adds freehand drawing with a customizable brush library, while Sketch to Shapes turns hand-drawn forms into editable vector shapes. Photo tools include RAW editing, non-destructive adjustments, and a Mask Tool designed to help trace difficult edges such as hair and fur with Apple Pencil. Elsewhere, layout tools support multi-page documents, master pages, and print-ready output.

Canva says the interface has been designed specifically for iPad rather than scaled down from the desktop app. As for Apple Pencil Pro support, it includes barrel roll, squeeze, and hover, alongside pressure and tilt controls.


The core sketching, vector, photo, and layout tools are free for individuals, but a free Canva account is required to use the app. The only paid-for features are the AI tools, which are locked behind a Canva premium plan – continuing the approach introduced with 2025's desktop relaunch.

The paid features are available through Canva AI Studio and include Generative Expand, image upscaling, noise reduction, and Decompose Layer, which splits a flat image into editable layers.

Affinity's website lists Books, Batch, Data Merge, Quick Adjustments, Info and Scope panels, macro recording, and Astrophotography Studio among the omissions, with more features planned over time.

available on the App Store as a free download with in-app purchases and requires iPadOS 18.0 or later.

title: Apple is now offering iPhone Duo replacements after widespread hinge issues
content:
Macworld





Amid all the excitement and crowds, iPhone Duo launch weekend didn’t go quite as well as Apple hoped. Some fans lucky enough to get their hands on a Duo on day one didn’t have the greatest experience with the new phone, as reports of inner screens cracking began popping up almost immediately. Here’s what’s happening, what Apple has said about the issue, and what you should do if your iPhone Duo starts having screen problems.
Update 11/2: Apple has notified stores of the issue with guidance for technicians on repair or replacement.
What’s the problem?
While many iPhone Duo users have had a flawless experience with their new phone, some users have had similar issues with horizontal and vertical lines appearing on the right-hand side of the inner screen. According to photos on Reddit and across social media, the issue presents itself as a thin vertical line down the middle of the screen accompanied by a thicker line extending horizontally across the right-hand side of the inner screen.
How common is it?
It’s unclear how many units are affected by the screen issue, but there have been widespread reports online from users as well as Apple Store demo units. Most users describe the issue occurring simply by opening their phone. One Reddit poster claimed they only had their phone ”for about six hours and had probably opened it fewer than 20 times.”
As far as we can tell, however, this problem hasn’t been noticed on any of the review units Apple sent out ahead of the launch, so it could be a manufacturing defect that only affected a certain batch of devices.

				
					

				
			Some iPhone Duo owners have experienced issues with the inner display.
Britta O’Boyle/Foundry




What is causing the problem?
It’s not completely clear what exactly is causing the issue, but it appears to be related to the hinge. To investigate the issue during its teardown, iFixit built an exact 3D hinge model and compared it with the reported damage locations. It reports:
The breaks cluster near the transition from the gap for the crossing flex cable to the central hinge support. The damage we’re seeing in photos isn’t right where the display cable passes through the hinge, but slightly lower, at a point where several edges meet and change how the thin display is supported as it bends. 
All those edges meeting in this spot mean lots of possible culprits. That center pivot looks different from the rest of the hinge. Could it be getting stuck? Could something else be getting stuck?
What we know is that the issues appear to all be causing identical screen problems, so it appears to be related to something under the display. 
Has Apple acknowledged the issue?
In a statement to the media, Apple says it is “aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units.” It recommends contacting AppleCare (1-800-APLCARE) for a replacement if a user experiences issues with their display. Apple has also issues a memo to Apple Stores and Apple Authorized Service Providers of the issue with guidance for technicians to diagnose the issue. 
There are numerous reports of Apple Stores swapping out affected units, but Apple hasn’t issued an official repair program. However, a support page titled “iPhone Duo Troubleshooting Hinge Issues” was published Sunday to offer “steps to help resolve issues,” including:
Device won’t open or close completely
Unexpected noise while opening or closing the device
Loose hinge
Bent or broken hinge
Enclosure damage that affects hinge operation
Apple suggests referring to the iPhone Duo user guide “for device hinge handling and safety guidance,” as well as removing third-party cases or screen protectors, and checking for “particles or dust along the hinge and for dents or scratches on the enclosure.”

				
					

				
			The iPhone Duo’s hinge is causing issues with the inner display on some models.
Britta O’Boyle




What can Duo users do?
While there isn’t an official replacement program yet, Apple says that phones will need to have the inner display assembly replaced. If your iPhone Duo has experienced any of the issues above, you should visit your local Apple Store or call Apple’s customer service number, 800-275-2273, or AppleCare, 1-800-275-2273 (1-800-APL-CARE).

title: Not every Apple product is ‘exciting,’ it turns out
content:
Macworld





Well, in the long list of Apple product launches, last week’s announcements were certainly some of them. Marketing supremo Greg Joswiak didn’t set the bar especially high when he predicted “an exciting week,” but even that comparatively tepid assessment turned out to be wildly optimistic.
The 8th-gen iPad mini falls, I would say, into the category of dull but worthwhile iterative refreshes. It gets some nice upgrades, including a thinner and lighter body, a faster processor, and an OLED screen, but doesn’t alter the fundamental truth that big-screen smartphones, and especially foldables, have rendered mid-price mini tablets largely obsolete… and thanks to another $100 price hike, the mini is now verging on premium. It needed a change of direction, not a costly glow-up.
Tuesday’s twin launches, presumably paired because neither was remotely enough to carry even a website update by itself, saw the arrival of M6 updates to the iMac and MacBook Pro. Apple found itself painfully short of “exciting” things to say about the new iMac; of the six things trumpeted in the summary paragraph at the top of the press release, four also apply to the previous M4 model. The same is basically true of the M6 MacBook Pro. The best we can say about them is that at least the prices are the same. 
It wasn’t until Wednesday that we got a launch that was genuinely groundbreaking (within the Apple ecosystem, at any rate), even if the touchscreen MacBook still strikes me as an offence against logic and reason.
It was a similar story earlier in October. There was one innovative if strategically questionable product, the HomeView, along with a worthy but straightforward new HomePod mini and an Apple TV refresh that costs way too much and has few exclusive features. The Apple Home Collection didn’t exactly set pulses racing either.
Traditionally, when there’s a big backlog of unreleased products, Apple follows its September event with another in October. We expected Apple to group together the Mac and iPad launches as it has so often in the past, build to the touchscreen MacBook as the flagship launch, and then very likely unveil HomeView as One More Thing. But for whatever reason it decided to go down a different route, splitting its remaining fall launches into a pair of low-key “experiences,” followed by a series of quiet press releases and site updates at the rate of one or two products per day. This seems to have become the company’s favored approach for anything less than its most high-profile launches, and there are advantages to making announcements in this way.
Most obviously, it saves on time and money because the marketing team doesn’t have to script and edit a 90-minute show, and busy senior execs don’t need to rehearse and perform a full-length presentation. But there’s the handy side effect that more obscure products get to enjoy their day in the sun. The new iPad mini would have been a minor footnote in the touchscreen MacBook show, for example, but instead it gets to bask in the glow of media and customer attention and be appreciated for the substantial (if in my opinion misguided) refresh that it is. If everything is rolled into an event, it’s inevitable that the smaller items will be lost in the hustle and bustle.
But that same hustle and bustle can sometimes do you a favor. The Apple TV’s missteps were cruelly exposed in the media spotlight, for example, and it might have been kinder to bury those perfunctory M6 micro-updates on a day when something more interesting was happening. 
Then there was the 2nd-gen HomePod mini, which essentially amounted to better AI (in a future software update) and worse colors. This was a necessary refresh, because the HomePod desperately needed Siri AI, and would likely have appeared in a few “important announcements you missed” articles if it was bottom of the bill at a big Apple event. But the HomePod mini was second on the bill at a very small event–sorry, experience–which drew attention to the fact Apple didn’t redesign the speaker or make any substantive non-AI-related upgrades six years after the first one came out. All that focus set a standard of noteworthiness it was never going to justify.
Not every Apple product is exciting, it turns out. But of course we knew that already. The company has found over the past decade or so that small iterative updates generally make the most sense from a financial point of view. The funny thing is that this fall has been unusually interesting: we’ve seen not one, not two, but three genuinely innovative Apple product launches in the form of the iPhone Duo, the HomeView, and the (touchscreen) MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. Yet the idiosyncratic manner in which the company has made its announcements has drawn attention to everything else.

title: Top Stories: Apple's Big MacBook Pro, iPad mini and iMac Updates
content:
One busy week after another for Apple has left our heads spinning, with this week seeing several Mac updates as well as a revamped iPad mini.


All of this week's craziness comes right on the heels of last Friday's iPhone Duo launch, not to mention all of the other products now available or still in pre-order status, so read on below for all of the details!

Top Stories

Everything Apple Announced This Week

It's been a busy October for Apple, and the company ended the month with a bang by introducing a number of new products even as some of the previously announced ones from earlier this month have yet to become available.


If you missed the news over the first three days of this week, we've rounded up all our coverage in one spot, so it's easy to take a look back. All of the new products are available for pre-order now, with a launch set for Friday, November 6.

Apple Announces OLED MacBook Pro With Touch Display

The headliner for the week was Wednesday's introduction of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. It's a mouthful, but it's the culmination of several years of rumors about a MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen, plus it includes several other upgrades such as lighter weights, a reinforced hinge to stabilize the display while it's being touched, a Dynamic Island instead of a notch, and even the return of an illuminated Apple logo on the lid.


The new machines are being sold alongside the previous MacBook Pro models with mini-LED displays, with the PROLED models carrying $400 price premiums over their counterparts even though they use the same M5 Pro and M5 Max chip options.

Apple Announces New 14-Inch MacBook Pro With M6 Chip

The low end of the MacBook Pro family also got an update this week, with Apple announcing a speed-bumped M6 version of the 14-inch base model.


The M6 chip in the ‌MacBook Pro‌ features a 12-core CPU with 2 super cores, 4 performance cores, and 6 efficiency cores, paired with a 12-core GPU. This is up from the M5 chip with a 10-core CPU with 4 super cores and 6 efficiency cores, paired with a 10-core GPU.

Alongside the M6 chip, the new 14-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌ now features support for Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 connectivity via Apple's N1 wireless chip. It can also now drive dual external 4K displays at up to 165Hz, up from 144Hz.

Apple Announces New iMac With M6 Chip and More

The 24-inch iMac also got a speed bump this week, with Apple's all-in-one desktop moving from the M4 chip to the M6 for faster performance and adding an N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support, faster SSD speeds, and more.


The new iMac has the same design as the previous model, and the color options remain the same: blue, green, pink, yellow, purple, orange, and silver.

Apple Announces New iPad Mini With 8.5-Inch OLED Display, A20 Pro Chip, and More

This week wasn't all about the Mac lineup, with Apple also taking the wraps off of a redesigned iPad mini featuring a larger 8.5-inch display that uses OLED technology for the first time.


In addition, the new iPad mini features a thinner and lighter design, an A20 Pro chip, a new Acoustic Display audio system that eliminates speaker holes, IP67-rated water and dust resistance, a landscape front camera, Apple's N1 chip with Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support, and more. Altogether, Apple says this amounts to the iPad mini's "biggest update ever."

Mac Studio With M5 Ultra Now Available With 512GB RAM for $22,299

When Apple introduced the M5 Max and M5 Ultra Mac Studio back in August, it said that a high-end M5 Ultra option with 512GB of memory would become available in late October, and it's finally here for an eye-popping price of $22,299.


This configuration is obviously only intended for hungriest of power users, requiring the highest-end chip with a 36-core CPU and 80-core GPU. The memory upgrade alone to increase from the standard 96GB to 512GB costs $15,500.

Crackgate? iPhone Duo Owners Report Screens Breaking Along the Hinge

With all of the announcements this week, it's easy to forget that the groundbreaking iPhone Duo just launched last Friday, and while early adopters have been enjoying much of what Apple's first foldable phone has to offer, it hasn't been entirely smooth sailing.


At least a few users have experienced sudden interior screen breakage seemingly caused by something going wrong in the complex hinge of the device. Apple has said that it is aware of the issue affecting "a small number of iPhone Duo units" and that affected users should contact AppleCare to obtain replacement units.

title: HomeView Software 27.2: Wallpapers, Control Center, and More
content:
Apple today released HomeView Software 27.2, which is the software that runs on the upcoming HomeView device set to launch on November 13.


The HomeView was announced earlier in October, but the early software release gives us a look at features like wallpapers and reveals a few tidbits we didn't previously know.

Wallpapers

There are 20 default wallpapers to choose from on HomeView, with a range of colors. Users will also likely be able to set their own photo wallpaper. The HomeView uses faces, but the wallpapers may be shown on the Home Screen.


View all 20 photos in the full article →

Face Editing

Guilherme Rambo shared an image of the HomeView's face editing interface, where users can choose the design they want to use on the HomeView's Lock Screen.


Of course I had to virtualize a HomeView 😅

Hello Screen

At startup, the HomeView will show the familiar "Hello" text.


Hello! https://t.co/pXdUR21Gev

Control Center

A HomeView setup animation shows Control Center on the HomeView.


HomeView setup animation found in HomeView Software 27.2 https://t.co/k4gCHNV3bY
— Aaron (@aaronp613) October 30, 2026



Light and Dark Mode

As with other Apple devices, the HomeView will have Light Mode and Dark Mode options, with the device able to swap between modes automatically based on time of day.

title: Apple's Flash Storage Suppliers Are Finally 'Getting Their Revenge'
content:
The Wall Street Journal's Rolfe Winkler this week reported that flash storage suppliers once "bullied" by Apple have been "getting their revenge" on the company over the past year due to a severe memory chip shortage, which stems from AI companies building out massive data centers that utilize significant amounts of flash storage and RAM.


As the iPhone took off, Apple became the world's largest buyer of flash storage, and naturally that gave the company a lot of leverage in negotiations.

Tony Blevins.

"After ordering flash at rock-bottom prices, Apple would refuse delivery at times if flash prices were falling," the report said. "That left suppliers holding piles of unsold chips, including ones custom-made for Apple. Kioxia executives joked they felt like Charlie Brown trying to kick the football—with Lucy always pulling it away."

Based in Japan, Kioxia was previously known as the Toshiba Memory Corporation.

Apple is also said to have "bullied flash makers into opening their books so it could monitor sales, making sure no one else got a better deal."

The report shared another example involving flash storage supplier Sandisk. Apple's other suppliers, such as SK Hynix and Samsung, were not mentioned.

"Around the end of 2015, Sandisk refused Apple's requests to send additional supply because it already had customers willing to pay more," the report said. "Blevins threatened a Sandisk salesman with retaliation, saying he would have Sandisk's chief executive, Sanjay Mehrotra, 'crawl on his knees' back to Apple, according to a person familiar with the call."

Things changed when the AI era arrived.

"Two years ago, Apple bought nearly twice the flash storage of Microsoft, Amazon, Meta and Google combined, according to TechInsights estimates," the report said, citing a research firm. "Hyperscalers are now buying double Apple's share."

raised prices on more than a dozen products this year, including iPhones, iPads, Macs, HomePods, the Apple TV, and more, with the company attributing these increases to the memory chip shortage. Apple's former CEO Tim Cook said price increases were "unavoidable."

Apple is not completely immune, though. Higher prices could result in lower demand, and the report said its profit margins on storage upgrades have been impacted. For example, TechInsights estimated that Apple makes a gross profit of $134 when a customer spends $200 to upgrade an iPhone 18 Pro from 256GB to 512GB of storage, down from $185 when a customer opted for the equivalent upgrade for the iPhone 17 Pro last year.

The Wall Street Journal. "We look forward to continuing our important work together."

will persist through 2030, so the pendulum may not swing back in Apple's direction for at least four more years. Eventually, though, it probably will.

title: 14 New Things Your iPhone Can Do in iOS 27.2
content:
Apple released iOS 27.2 on October 26, bringing enhancements to Siri AI, adding Suggestions in Messages, and sneaking in a string of smaller additions across Photos, Podcasts, Games, Apple TV, and FaceTime. 


iOS 27.2 is available to download to your device now via Settings ➝ General ➝ Software Update. Note that some features may not be available in all regions or on all iPhone models. Apple maintains a feature availability list with all the details.

Ask Siri About Past Conversations


Siri AI can now recall your past conversations, so you can ask it about something it told you before, like the restaurants it recommended last week. Siri AI features require an iPhone 16 model or later, or an iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 15 Pro Max.

Get Answers From More of Your Personal Context


Siri AI can now draw from more sources when answering, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, and your voicemails. Apple says you'll also get better results from Safari history and Reading List.

Use Siri in More Languages


Siri AI now supports French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish, in addition to English. Just keep in mind that, as things stand, it's not available in the EU or mainland China.

Control Which Apps Siri and Search Can Access


A new settings menu has been added that lets you choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access, all from one list. You can find it in Settings ➝ Siri ➝ Excluded Apps.

Copy Just Part of a Siri Response


Granular text selection lets you select and copy only the part of a Siri response you need, rather than the whole reply.

Act on Suggestions in Messages


held back from the initial release, so its arrival has been a good while coming.

Manage Shared Albums More Easily


Shared Albums in Photos gain three additions. You can now edit captions and comments, the app can avoid adding duplicate photos, and it can display a reminder before an album expires so participants can save important photos and videos.

Spot AI-Generated Images


iOS 27.2 supports SynthID watermarking, which aims to help you identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground.

See What Your Friends Are Playing


In the Games app, the Friends tab now provides context around friend suggestions, plus it shows you any recent games your friends have played on their player pages.

Create Apple TV Profiles for Your Household


If you have an Apple TV, you can now create profiles in the account settings section on iPhone and iPad. All you need for a profile is a name, plus whether it's for an adult or a child. Creating a profile for a child limits content to a PG rating by default, but there's a customize option for finer control. You can select age ratings for TV shows and movies that are appropriate for the child based on their age.

Stream FaceTime From Front and Rear Cameras


Dual Capture is now available in group ‌FaceTime‌ calls, so you can stream ‌FaceTime‌ video content from the front and rear cameras at the same time. On a compatible device running ‌iOS 27‌.2, flipping the camera while on a ‌FaceTime‌ call automatically turns on Dual Capture.

Dual Capture is available on the iPhone 17, ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro, ‌iPhone 17‌ Pro Max, iPhone Air, iPhone 18 Pro, ‌iPhone 18 Pro‌ Max, and ‌iPhone Duo‌.

Watch Several Live Sports Streams at Once


Multiview has been expanded in the Apple TV app to the iPhone, so you can now watch up to four live sports streams at the same time. Multiview works for sports events that come with an ‌Apple TV‌ subscription, so that's Major League Soccer (MLS), Formula 1 (F1) in the U.S., and Friday Night Baseball doubleheaders during the Major League Baseball season.

iPhone Duo Edge Light and Apple Pencil Support
 

iOS 27.2 adds Apple Pencil USB-C support to the ‌iPhone Duo‌. It also includes support for the Edge Light feature that first appeared in macOS to illuminate your face during video calls.

Be Reminded of a Contact's Anniversary on a Call

title: iPhone Duo Review: One Week Later
content:
It's been a week since the iPhone Duo was released, and MacRumors videographer Dan Barbera wanted to revisit his review since he's been able to use the Duo for a longer stretch of time.

Subscribe to the MacRumors YouTube channel for more videos.

You've probably seen images of iPhone Duos with a bright white line running across one side of the inner display. There is a defect affecting some users, but Apple says it's a problem limited to a small number of units.

MacRumors have had a display crack, and we've seen some AI photos floating around, so it's hard to tell just how many people are actually having problems. iPhone Duos with the hinge issue that causes the display to crack seem to get damaged shortly after purchase, so if you've had an ‌iPhone Duo‌ for the last week and it's still fine, it's not likely to have this defect.

The outer display is small, but Dan finds it useful for checking notifications, replying to messages, and scrolling through apps and websites. He unfolds it for multitasking or longer messages, and is a fan of using the ‌iPhone Duo‌ unfolded in portrait mode for watching videos and using an app at the same time.

Touch ID fingerprint sensor easy to find, and says Apple Watch unlock is similar to Face ID. The cameras are just okay, and someone who zooms in a lot is probably going to miss having a telephoto lens.

iPhone 18 Pro and a Pro Max, and for most people, it's likely going to last a full day. Not all apps have been updated for the Duo layout yet, but it's getting better. There's an extension called Wider that extends the Safari window to the edges of the ‌iPhone Duo‌'s outer display, and it's a big improvement. We may see other accommodations in the coming months as developers and users get used to the new layout.

Dan says the ‌iPhone Duo‌ is the most excited he's been about an iPhone in a long time, and he plans to keep using it even though he misses having a telephoto lens.

On this week's episode of The MacRumors Show, we discuss Apple's newly announced OLED MacBook Pro, iPad mini with A20 Pro, and M6 versions of the iMac and entry-level 14-inch ‌MacBook Pro‌.

Subscribe to The MacRumors Show YouTube channel for more videos

The MacBook Pro gains a tandem ‌OLED‌ display with touch support for the first time. Available in 14- and 16-inch sizes, the "PROLED XDR display" offers up to 2,000 nits of peak HDR and SDR brightness, a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio, and Adobe RGB support alongside P3. Touch input enables gestures such as scrolling, pinching to zoom, and dragging content, with a reinforced hinge and camera stabilization designed to accommodate interaction with the screen.

Dynamic Island replaces the notch, providing access to Live Activities, Siri AI, and more. The enclosure is thinner and lighter, with the 14-inch model weighing 3 pounds and the 16-inch model weighing 4 pounds. The larger model's display grows to 16.3 inches, and the iconic illuminated Apple logo returns.

upgraded speakers with 50% deeper bass and dedicated tuning for closed-lid playback. Maximum storage doubles to 16TB. Pricing starts at $2,899 for the 14-inch model and $3,399 for the 16-inch model, a $400 premium over comparable mini-LED configurations.

nano-texture option on the 256GB and 512GB configurations. It is thinner and lighter at 5.4mm thick, and becomes the first iPad with an official IP67 water and dust resistance rating. The display remains limited to 60Hz, with no ProMotion support.

additional CPU core and a second 16-core Neural Engine compared with the 128GB and 256GB models.

Acoustic Display speaker system eliminates external speaker holes, while the front camera moves to the landscape edge and the rear camera gains an Adaptive True Tone flash. Other additions include fast charging, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, Apple's C2 modem on cellular models, and extended external display support with iPadOS 27.2. The ‌iPad mini‌ starts at $699 in Midnight or Starlight, with a new $79 TechWoven Smart Folio available separately.

M6 iMac replaces the M4 model, adding two CPU and GPU cores to both the two-port and four-port configurations. It also gains GPU Neural Accelerators, dual 16-core Neural Engines, up to twice as fast SSD storage, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, and 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet. Pricing starts at $1,499, with the four-port model starting at $1,699.

14-inch MacBook Pro moves from M5 to M6, with a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU, dual 16-core Neural Engines, and upgraded wireless connectivity. Memory bandwidth increases to 170GB/s on 24GB and 32GB configurations, while the 16GB model remains at 153GB/s. Its $1,999 starting price and battery life of up to 24 hours carry over from the outgoing model.

title: Ternus talks AI, Steve Jobs, and not looking to emulate business CEOs
content:
CEO John Ternus has been doing the rounds promoting the new MacBook Pro, but has now also taken questions about his approach to Apple's business approach.


John Ternus
Even as Ternus has been saying that now is the right time to produce a touch-screen MacBook Pro, he is still being asked about being CEO. Wired's Steven Levy says Ternus was stumped by a question about business leaders who inspire him.
"I haven't really thought about that," he said. "Of course I've read books, but there's so much to be learned from the people I get to work with."

How to get Apple TV

content:
It's Halloween, so it's a great time to make sure you're not getting tricked out of your hard-earned cash and cancel those subscriptions you've forgotten about. Here's how to do it.


Why and how you should audit your subscriptions
Digital hygiene, the practice of keeping a clean, safe digital footprint, is critical for anyone who uses the internet — which is pretty much everyone. Many things fall under the digital hygiene umbrella, from responsible email management to removing your data from data brokerage companies' websites.
There are many digital hygiene tasks you should do at least twice a year. For instance, you're probably going to want to check to make sure none of your passwords have wound up in a data breach.

title: Don’t wait for Black Friday: This AirTag bundle deal is as good as it gets
content:
Macworld





		
Apple AirTag 2nd Gen
View Deal
If you have an iPhone and carry around keys, a bag, or anything else that might be lost, the best thing you can get is a four-pack of AirTags. Normally $99, Apple’s 2nd-gen AirTags are a great way to keep track of the things that don’t have Apple logos. And today they’re an absolute steal: Amazon has slashed the price of the AirTags 4-pack to $70 for the very first time, 30 percent off the usual $99 and much lower than the previous best price.
AirTags are super easy to use and, compared to the previous generation, they’re louder and more accurate, allowing you to better keep track of your belongings. Hook one of these up to your keys and, instead of wasting 10 minutes looking for them in the morning, you can just make the tag sing you the song of its people, making it easier to locate. You can also slip one into your wallet, drop one into your suitcase, and tuck one into your kid’s backpack, each showing up in the Find My app.
When you leave something behind that’s out of the range of your phone, AirTag will ping other nearby iOS devices to let you see its location in the app and track it down quickly. As long as it has battery life—which lasts for more than a year with a standard CR2032 3V lithium coin battery, it’ll report its location in an instant.
This deal drops the cost of a single AirTag down to  $17.50, an impressive $11.50 lower than what you’d pay for a single AirTag through Apple. At an all-time low, there’s really no reason to wait any longer to buy yourself a new set of AirTags because it’s unlikely you’ll get a better deal than this one, even on Black Friday.

title: How to turn a Siri Remote into a handy Mac controller
content:
A Siri Remote can make controlling a Mac from across the room much easier, and with one utility you can use it as a small trackpad, although you'll need more than macOS's built-in support to get the full experience.

Siri Remote with Mac
If your Mac mini is connected to a TV, or you use your MacBook for presentations, reaching for a keyboard to control playback isn't always convenient. An Apple TV Siri Remote lets you manage basic controls from across the room without returning to your Mac.
A Siri Remote connects to a Mac over Bluetooth, and macOS already supports some of its buttons. However, Apple designed the remote for Apple TV, so its clickpad doesn't automatically control the mouse or navigate Mac apps.
Basic controls work without additional software, while third-party apps add more functionality. Whether it's worth setting up depends on how much control you need and whether you're willing to switch the remote between your Mac and Apple TV.

content:
Apple chose to have perhaps four times more iPhone Duo stock at retail than for sale online on launch day, and even so, most went home empty-handed.

Apple described demand for the iPhone Duo as being "extraordinary," and manufacturer Foxconn has talked about using its international facilities to produce more. Certainly the pre-order stock sold out instantaneously, although a new report suggests there was a reason for that.

title: Russia Places Apple on State Surveillance Registry
content:
Apple faces Russian data retention and disclosure requirements after being added to the country's state surveillance registry, Bloomberg reports.


Russia's communications regulator, Roskomnadzor, listed Apple and Microsoft on October 2 as "organizers of information dissemination," a classification that carries obligations to preserve communications and make data available to Russian security agencies.

Those obligations cover correspondence and messages containing audio or video. Companies must also keep information identifying users and recording the transmission of their communications within Russia for three years. Businesses that fail to meet the requirements risk fines and, ultimately, restrictions on their services.

Apple and Microsoft join other services on the registry, including WhatsApp, Telegram, and Snapchat. Google and its Meet video calling service were listed in January.

December 2025 block on FaceTime. Roskomnadzor justified that restriction by alleging the service was being used to facilitate terrorism, recruitment, and fraud. Russia had already restricted calling through WhatsApp and Telegram and blocked Signal and Viber.

content:
Today is HomePod mini 2 launch day, with the first pre-orders beginning to arrive to customers and the speaker now available to purchase at most Apple Store locations around the world. In the U.S., the HomePod mini 2 is priced at $149, with two-tone pink, green, and blue color options available alongside white and midnight.


Here is what is new with the HomePod mini 2:

Siri AI support is coming in a future software update, with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad required for requests involving your personal context.

S10 chip, up from the S5 chip for the previous model. Apple said the S10 chip enables "advanced computational audio," but it did not explicitly confirm if the HomePod mini 2 has improved sound quality compared to the original model.

Bluetooth 6 support, up from Bluetooth 5 for the previous model.

Default audio output support on Macs with Wi-Fi 6E and later. The full-sized HomePod 2 also supports this capability with the latest software updates.

Sound Glow: the top area glows and pulses in sync with the music playing. This feature has also been added to the original HomePod mini.

Four-speaker surround sound with the new Apple TV 4K: connect four HomePod mini 2 and/or full-sized HomePod 2 speakers in front and rear pairs. A related Whole Room Audio feature is offered for parties.

Three microphones for Siri, down from four in the previous model. It is unclear if users will notice this difference.

Two-tone pink, green, and blue color options, along with white and midnight.

3% weight reduction. Huge.
The previous HomePod mini was initially $99, but it became $129 after a June price increase. As mentioned, the new model is $149.

title: Rian Johnson's iPhone Camera App Goes Viral
content:
Filmmaker Rian Johnson, best known for writing and directing "Knives Out," "Glass Onion," and "Star Wars: The Last Jedi," has seen his new iPhone photography app Chromagraph Camera climb to the top of the paid App Store charts after attracting attention on social media this week.


Johnson developed the app with his longtime cinematographer Steve Yedlin and programmer Eric Cameron, bringing image processing techniques from their films to iPhone still photography. Chromagraph currently ranks No. 1 in Photo & Video on the U.S. App Store.

Johnson's announcement on X accumulated six million views within a day, while users have been sharing their results, with some photo posts attracting thousands of likes.





Chromagraph shoots RAW photos and processes them using techniques Yedlin developed for his films, giving pictures a distinctive treatment of color, contrast, and grain. It also adds halation, a soft glow around bright areas. Users can adjust the look with controls for color, tone, and texture.

The effect appears after taking a photo, when users open the app's gallery. Original RAW files are kept intact, so edits can be changed later.

For sharing, photographs can be exported as JPEG or HEIC files with the processing applied. An automatic export option also sends each finished photo to the user's photo library.

App Store and requires iOS 17 or later.

title: Got a Mac Pro collecting dust? This kit will convert it into a Windows PC
content:
Macworld





If you have an old “cheese-grater” Mac Pro, you probably don’t want to part with it. You look at it and wonder what you’re going to do with it, since it can’t be upgraded. Seems like a waste to throw it out, and you won’t get nearly enough to make it worth selling. Well, a Canadian mechatronics enthusiast understands your predicament and has set out to do something about it.
Stefan Bond has launched the Mac Pro 7,1 (A1991) ATX Conversion Kit project on Kickstarter. The kit can be used to install “modern PC hardware” into the chassis of a Mac Pro–specifically, the Mac Pro that was introduced in 2019 and identified with the model number 7,1. Since it was built with Mac hardware in mind, you can’t simply gut it and pop in a PC motherboard, a gigantic graphics card, and other components. The Conversion Kit will allow you to do that by providing a main motherboard and PSU mounting plate, hard drive sled assemblies and cables, Mac Pro fan-adapter PCBs, and more.
To be clear, this is a kit that enables you to install PC components (which aren’t included) for building a PC that runs Windows. There’s no official way to upgrade the Mac Pro with Apple components. If you really want to run macOS, you should be able to turn this into a Hackintosh after building it.
Bond has a goal of $10,000 for his Kickstarter, and a bid of $699 in Canadian currency (about $500 in the U.S.) gets you a full conversion kit. If you don’t have a Mac Pro but just want to contribute to the spirit of the project, you can chip in CA$10, and your name will be mentioned in the final project video.
Apple discontinued the Mac Pro earlier this year, ending a 20-year run for the Mac Pro brand. The latest time it was updated was in 2023, when Apple released it with an M2 Ultra chip. When this design was introduced in 2019, it had Intel processors. Apple offers the Mac Studio as its top Mac workstation, but it doesn’t have anywhere near the character of its old metal towers.

title: Touch isn’t the killer feature of the new MacBook Pro
content:
Macworld





Apple has finally brought a touch interface to the Mac, 43 years after the first commercial PC with a touchscreen, the HP 150. It’s a momentous event in Apple history, one that longtime Mac users never thought would come.
The new laptop is going to be mainly referred to as the “touchscreen MacBook Pro,” and there’s a lot of talk about the feature. But if you think of the new laptop only in terms of Touch, you’re missing the point. There’s a reason why Apple calls it the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. It’s clumsy and lengthy, but notice how “Touch” isn’t one of the words.
“Touch” isn’t in the name because it’s not the most important new feature of the new MacBook Pro. In fact, Apple has a link to a white paper about the PROLED Display on the product wesbite, and Touch isn’t mentioned at all. I think it’s the least important feature, and there are other aspects of the laptop that are more important and have implications for other MacBooks down the line.
OLED takes the lead
The display is the most important feature, but not because of touch, but because it’s a tandem OLED display that can “deliver the kind of visual fidelity pros have been dreaming of,” according to Apple. Considering Apple’s long history of producing the best quality laptop displays, I’m inclined to believe that statement.

				
					

				
			
Apple




Look at these specs. This is on a laptop? Damn.
10,000,000:1 contrast ratio
XDR brightness: Up to 1000 nits sustained full-screen; 2000 nits peak (HDR content only)
SDR brightness: Up to 1000 nits sustained full-screen; 2000 nits peak (outdoor)
ProMotion adaptive refresh rates
1.00 percent reflectance, lower than traditional OLED displays
P3 + Adobe RGB wide color gamuts
Apple Color-Matching Functions 2026
Medical imaging support





That’s easily one of the best, if not the best display ever put in a laptop. Can a display on a laptop be so good-looking that you’ll never want to take your eyes off it? If it can, count on Apple to make it. 
What’s even more exciting is what it means for the rest of the MacBook lineup in the future. Several reports have said OLED is coming to the MacBook Air, possibly in 2028, and though it probably won’t be on the same level as the MacBook Pro with PROLED Display—consider the difference between the iPad mini and the iPad Pro—it’ll still be a major upgrade from the current LED-backlit IPS panel.
Lighter design
A few days ago, I was in the office with my 16-inch MacBook Pro in my backpack. I put my backpack on my desk, and it landed with a loud thud. My co-worker (a PC fanboy) was shocked. “What’s with the rocks in your bag?” he exclaimed
The new MacBook Pro is nearly a pound lighter. That might not sound like much, but it makes a difference if you’re moving around often, or if you’re like me and you have an hour-long commute on public transportation. Hopefully, that thud won’t be as resonant with the new laptop.
It’ll be interesting to see if the advances Apple made to achieve the smaller and lighter MacBook Pro will carry over to the other MacBooks. Imagine if the MacBook Neo and the 13-inch MacBook Air, Apple’s lightest laptops at 2.7 pounds, were closer to 2 pounds. 
Dynamic Island
The notch on the MacBooks is there because the bezel is too thin to fit the FaceTime camera, but it’s also just sort of… there. It’s not really obtrusive, because it sits above the usable screen space in the status bar, but it still feels like a vestigial part of the laptop with no real purpose.

				
					

				
			
Apple




The Dynamic Island replaces the notch, and it’s now a functional anchor of the Mac. It works as it does on the iPhone, so you know it’ll be a useful home for Spotlight search and Lite Activities. I’ve come to appreciate how it’s used on the iPhone, so I’m excited to see it become a natural extension of macOS.
Will the Dynamic Island make it to other MacBooks? It would be a shame if Apple decided it was a premium feature for only the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, but I can see that happening. Apple won’t switch from the notch to the Dynamic Island until the other MacBooks upgrade their display tech, so we won’t know for some time.
Glowing Apple logo
It’s just a logo, but as Mac users and Apple fans, that Apple logo has meaning. When the glowing Apple was introduced in the 1999 PowerBook G3, it made a statement (even though it was upside down for the first couple of years). It told people we were proud Mac users. We mourned the loss of the logo in 2015.
But the glowing logo and the statement it brings are back. But this time it comes as a flex, the way that Cosmic Orange was for the iPhone 17 Pro. People who know Macs will see it and know you’ve got the new MacBook Pro. As for the people who don’t know Macs, well, they’ll see it and be envious. Best of all, the glowing Apple icon won’t be upside down when the lid is open. And now that it’s a little screen of its own, you can even turn it off if you want.

title: Where Did All the iPhone Duos Go? Mostly to Apple's Stores
content:
Apple allocated roughly 80% of its initial iPhone Duo inventory to its retail stores, with locations holding as few as 50 units each, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman. 


Speaking on the latest episode of his Power On podcast, Gurman, citing people very close to the device's logistics, said most customers who bought a Duo in store on day one got one by waiting in line. 

pre-orders slipped to late January within minutes on October 16, while most people who queued on launch day walked away with a new phone.

At the time, Apple described demand as "nothing short of extraordinary" and said it was working to satisfy demand "as quickly as possible," so there's a good chance that, even if a delivery estimate for your order is way out in the future, it could improve over time.
